docs.title: About this book
docs.text: A textbook on describing digital hardware: the register transfer level, Verilog and VHDL side by side, and the open RISC-V instruction set, ending with a small RISC-V processor written in Verilog. Worked examples, traces, figures and exercises with folded answers.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Buses, Memory, Datapath and Control
docs.text: Chapter 1 gave us registers and the microoperations that move data between them. This chapter shows how many registers share their wires, how a whole memory fits into the same notation, and how every RTL design splits into a part that holds data (the datapath) and a part that decides what happens to it (the control unit). It closes with a complete worked design, a machine that computes the greatest common divisor, and with the first look at how an RTL description turns into a hardware description language.

docs.title: 2.1 Buses
docs.text:
If every register could talk to every other register through its own private wires, a machine with \(n\) registers would need \(n(n-1)\) one-way paths. Four 8-bit registers would need 12 paths of 8 wires each, 96 wires in all, and a sixteen-register machine would need 240 paths. Real machines share wiring through a bus: one common set of wires that, at any moment, carries the value of exactly one chosen register, and from which any register may load. Four 8-bit registers on one bus need only 8 wires, plus a few control lines to choose the source.

There are two classic ways of building a bus.

docs.title: The multiplexer bus
docs.text:
A bank of multiplexers, one per bit, selects which register drives the bus. With four registers, a 4-to-1 multiplexer on each bit chooses among R0 to R3, using two select lines S1 S0. Any register whose load signal is 1 copies the bus at the next clock edge (Figure 2.1). This form is purely combinational, it can never short-circuit, and it is what synthesis tools actually build from an HDL description.

Figure 2.1. A bus built from a multiplexer. The select lines S1 S0 choose which register drives the bus; every register whose load signal is 1 copies the bus at the next edge.

docs.title: The tri-state bus
docs.text:
In the second form each register reaches the bus through a three-state buffer. When enabled, the buffer passes its register's value; when disabled, its output is in the high-impedance state, written Z, which is electrically a disconnection. This saves logic on a long physical bus, but the control must guarantee that exactly one buffer is enabled at a time. Two drivers fighting, one pushing a 1 and the other a 0, is a short circuit. Inside a chip, tools build the multiplexer form; tri-state buses belong to board-level wiring and chip pins.

A bus transfer is written like any other transfer, naming the bus when it matters:

BUS <- R1,  R2 <- BUS        put R1 on the bus, load it into R2
R2 <- R1                     shorthand for the same thing, when the bus is implied

docs.title: 2.2 Memory
docs.text:
Memory is treated as one large array of registers, addressed through an address register AR. Mano's notation writes M[AR] for "the memory word that AR selects". A read copies the addressed word into a data register, and a write overwrites it:

Read:   DR <- M[AR]       load the data register from the addressed word
Write:  M[AR] <- R1       store R1 into the addressed word

Both take one clock pulse, and both are microoperations like any other.

Example 2.1: which address does a read use?

In one clock pulse the transfers DR ← M[AR], AR ← AR + 1 are performed. Which word is read?

  1. Every right-hand side is sampled before any register is written.
  2. So M[AR] is evaluated with AR as it was when the pulse began, the old address.
  3. The increment lands at the same edge, leaving AR pointing at the next word, ready for the next read.

This is exactly how a processor steps through consecutive words of memory, and it is why AR and DR can safely be changed in the same pulse as the read.

docs.title: 2.3 Datapath and control
docs.text:
An RTL system divides cleanly into two cooperating parts (Figure 2.2).

  • The datapath is where data lives and is transformed: the registers, the ALU, shifters, buses and multiplexers. It answers what can be computed.
  • The control unit is a finite state machine, a circuit that is always in one of a few named states and moves between them on clock edges. It watches status flags coming back from the datapath (for example, "the result was zero"), an instruction's opcode or a counter, and on every cycle asserts the control signals that make the datapath perform the right microoperation. It answers in what order.
Figure 2.2. Every RTL design has a datapath, which holds and transforms data, and a control unit, which sends control signals to it and reads status back.

Return to the conditional transfer P: R2 ← R1. The P is a control signal. Somewhere in the datapath it enables the load line of R2 and steers the multiplexers so that R1 is on the bus. The control unit's whole job is to produce a correctly timed sequence of such signals. The datapath is the orchestra and the control unit is the conductor; neither makes music alone.

docs.title: Control as a schedule of signals
docs.text:
Take a tiny machine that adds the word at memory address 20 to the accumulator. Each row of the following table is one clock cycle, and the control unit asserts the signals on that row.

Cycle Microoperation Signals the control unit raises T0 AR ← 20 select the constant 20 onto the bus; load AR T1 DR ← M[AR] memory read; load DR T2 ACC ← ACC + DR ALU operation = add; load ACC T3 (done) return to waiting

Almost every hardware bug turns out to be this: the right signal, on the wrong cycle.

docs.title: Two ways to build a control unit
docs.text:
Hardwired control Microprogrammed control How signals are generated Gates and a state register compute every control signal directly A small ROM stores one word per step; the bits of the word are the control signals Speed Fast Slower: an extra memory read at each step Changing it Redesign the logic Rewrite the ROM Typical home Simple, fast processors with a small and regular instruction set Older processors with large and complicated instruction sets

When you write a state machine in Verilog or VHDL, you are writing hardwired control.

docs.title: 2.4 From RTL to a hardware description language
docs.text:
Here the notation pays off, because a single register transfer maps almost mechanically onto both Verilog and VHDL. Consider an accumulator that adds a data register into itself when the control signal load is 1. Mano would write load: ACC ← ACC + DR. The same microoperation in three notations:

load: ACC <- ACC + DR

module accumulator (
    input        clk,
    input        load,
    input  [7:0] DR,
    output reg [7:0] ACC
);
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        if (load)
            ACC <= ACC + DR;     // load: ACC <- ACC + DR
    end
endmodule

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;
use ieee.numeric_std.all;

entity accumulator is
    port ( clk  : in  std_logic;
           load : in  std_logic;
           DR   : in  unsigned(7 downto 0);
           ACC  : out unsigned(7 downto 0) );
end accumulator;

architecture rtl of accumulator is
    signal acc_r : unsigned(7 downto 0) := (others => '0');
begin
    process (clk)
    begin
        if rising_edge(clk) then
            if load = '1' then
                acc_r <= acc_r + DR;     -- load: ACC <- ACC + DR
            end if;
        end if;
    end process;
    ACC <= acc_r;
end rtl;

Read the three side by side and the correspondence is complete:

In RTL In Verilog In VHDL "at the next clock edge" always @(posedge clk) if rising_edge(clk) the control function load: if (load) if load = '1' then the arrow ← <= <=

Learning a second language is therefore mostly learning a new spelling of three ideas you already have: the clock edge, the condition and the transfer. The arrow becomes the non-blocking assignment <= in Verilog and the signal assignment <= in VHDL, both of which defer the write to the end of the time step, so that all right-hand sides are read first. That is precisely the "read everything, then write everything" rule of the previous chapter.

Why not the blocking assignment?

A blocking assignment = in Verilog takes effect immediately, like a statement in a program. In the swap R1 ← R2, R2 ← R1 it would copy R2 into R1 first and then copy the new R1 back, leaving both registers equal. Chapters 3 and 4 treat the two kinds of assignment in detail.

docs.title: 2.5 A worked design: a greatest-common-divisor machine
docs.text:
The three levels of Chapter 1 described a machine that finds the greatest common divisor of \(A\) and \(B\) by repeated subtraction. We now design it properly, as a datapath and a control unit.

Algorithm. While \(A \ne B\): if \(A > B\) replace \(A\) by \(A - B\), otherwise replace \(B\) by \(B - A\). When \(A = B\), that common value is the greatest common divisor. (The algorithm assumes both inputs are positive. If either were zero the subtraction would never make progress.)

Datapath. Two registers A and B, a comparator that reports whether \(A = B\) or \(A > B\), and a subtractor in front of each register. The status signals returned to the control unit are A == B and A > B.

Control. One state to wait for a start request, one to load the inputs, one to compare, one to subtract each way, and one to announce that the result is ready (Figure 2.3).

Figure 2.3. The control states of the GCD machine. SUBA and SUBB both return to CMP; DONE returns to IDLE.

The microoperations belonging to each state, in Mano's notation, are:

State Control function Microoperation Next state IDLE — none LOAD if start, else IDLE LOAD S_LOAD A ← x, B ← y CMP CMP — none DONE if \(A = B\); SUBA if \(A > B\); otherwise SUBB SUBA S_SUBA A ← A − B CMP SUBB S_SUBB B ← B − A CMP DONE — none (done = 1) IDLE once start is low

The table converts directly into code, using the three-block structure that Chapter 4 explains: a state register, next-state logic, and the datapath registers with their outputs.

module gcd #(parameter W = 8) (
    input  wire         clk,
    input  wire         rst_n,
    input  wire         start,
    input  wire [W-1:0] x,
    input  wire [W-1:0] y,
    output wire [W-1:0] result,
    output wire         done
);
    localparam [2:0] S_IDLE = 3'd0, S_LOAD = 3'd1, S_CMP  = 3'd2,
                     S_SUBA = 3'd3, S_SUBB = 3'd4, S_DONE = 3'd5;

    reg [2:0]   state, next;
    reg [W-1:0] A, B;

    // control: state register
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
        if (!rst_n) state <= S_IDLE;
        else        state <= next;

    // control: next-state logic
    always @(*) begin
        next = state;
        case (state)
            S_IDLE: if (start) next = S_LOAD;
            S_LOAD: next = S_CMP;
            S_CMP:  if (A == B)     next = S_DONE;
                    else if (A > B) next = S_SUBA;
                    else            next = S_SUBB;
            S_SUBA: next = S_CMP;
            S_SUBB: next = S_CMP;
            S_DONE: if (!start) next = S_IDLE;
            default: next = S_IDLE;
        endcase
    end

    // datapath: the registers and their microoperations
    always @(posedge clk) begin
        case (state)
            S_LOAD: begin A <= x; B <= y; end
            S_SUBA: A <= A - B;
            S_SUBB: B <= B - A;
            default: ;
        endcase
    end

    assign result = A;
    assign done   = (state == S_DONE);
endmodule

Example 2.2: tracing gcd(12, 18)

Let x = 12, y = 18 and start = 1. Each row is one clock cycle: the state the machine is in during the cycle, the microoperation of that state, and the register contents after the edge that ends the cycle.

Cycle State Microoperation \(A\) after \(B\) after Decision for the next state 0 IDLE none ? ? start = 1, go to LOAD 1 LOAD A ← 12, B ← 18 12 18 go to CMP 2 CMP none 12 18 \(A < B\), go to SUBB 3 SUBB B ← 18 − 12 12 6 go to CMP 4 CMP none 12 6 \(A > B\), go to SUBA 5 SUBA A ← 12 − 6 6 6 go to CMP 6 CMP none 6 6 \(A = B\), go to DONE 7 DONE none 6 6 done = 1, result = 6

The machine announces its answer, \(6\), seven clock cycles after it left IDLE. Notice that the datapath registers change only in the three states that name a microoperation, and that the decisions in CMP read the status of the registers as they stand at the start of the cycle.

The design shows the division of labour clearly. The always @(*) block is purely the schedule: it never touches A or B. The clocked block with the case is purely the datapath: it never decides what comes next. Almost every controller in a real chip, from a UART to a memory controller, has this shape.

docs.title: 2.6 Summary
docs.text:
• A bus is one set of shared wires carrying one register at a time. A multiplexer bus is purely combinational and is what synthesis builds; a tri-state bus needs control that guarantees one driver.
  • Memory is a large array of registers addressed through AR; M[AR] names the addressed word, and a read or a write is an ordinary microoperation. A read in a pulse uses the address as it was at the start of the pulse.
  • Every design divides into a datapath (what can be computed) and a control unit (in what order), the control unit being a finite state machine that may be hardwired or microprogrammed.
  • A conditional transfer maps almost mechanically onto HDL: the edge, the condition and the arrow each acquire a spelling.
  • A small machine such as the GCD unit is designed by listing the registers, the status signals, the states with their microoperations and the next-state decisions, and then writing the three parts of the code.

docs.title: 2.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 2.1. Eight 16-bit registers must be able to exchange data. How many wires does direct wiring of every pair need, and how many data wires does a multiplexer bus need? How many select lines does the bus multiplexer need?

Answer

Direct wiring needs \(n(n-1) = 8 \times 7 = 56\) one-way paths of 16 wires, which is \(896\) wires. A bus needs only 16 data wires. To choose among 8 sources the multiplexer needs \(\lceil \log_2 8 \rceil = 3\) select lines.

Exercise 2.2. Write the control schedule (cycle, microoperation, signals raised) for the instruction "add the contents of the memory word whose address is in AR to ACC, then increment AR". Can the increment share a cycle with another step?

Answer

One possible schedule uses three cycles. T0: DR ← M[AR] (memory read, load DR). T1: ACC ← ACC + DR (ALU add, load ACC). T2: AR ← AR + 1 (increment, load AR). The increment can share a cycle with the read, because the read samples AR at the start of the pulse: DR ← M[AR], AR ← AR + 1 in T0 is legal (Example 2.1), which shortens the schedule to two cycles.

Exercise 2.3. A word in memory is to be incremented in place: M[AR] ← M[AR] + 1. Memory has a single port, so only one access is possible per cycle. Give a sequence of microoperations that does it.

Answer

Memory cannot be read and written in the same cycle, so the update is split into three steps. T0: DR ← M[AR] (read). T1: DR ← DR + 1 (use the ALU). T2: M[AR] ← DR (write back). AR does not change during the sequence.

Exercise 2.4. Trace the GCD machine of Section 2.5 for x = 9, y = 6, giving the contents of A and B after each LOAD, SUBA and SUBB cycle and the final result.

Answer

After LOAD: \(A = 9\), \(B = 6\). In CMP, \(A > B\), so SUBA: \(A = 9 - 6 = 3\). In CMP, \(A < B\) (\(3 < 6\)), so SUBB: \(B = 6 - 3 = 3\). In CMP, \(A = B\), so the machine goes to DONE with result = 3, and \(\gcd(9, 6) = 3\).

Exercise 2.5. What does the GCD machine do if x = 0 and y = 5? Suggest a change that makes the design safe, and say where in the design it belongs.

Answer

After LOAD, \(A = 0\) and \(B = 5\). In every CMP cycle \(A < B\), so the machine enters SUBB and computes \(B \leftarrow 5 - 0 = 5\), again and again, and never reaches DONE. The fix belongs in the control: in LOAD (or in CMP) test whether either register is zero and, if so, go to DONE at once, with a convention such as returning the other operand, since \(\gcd(0, n) = n\). This adds one status signal (A == 0, B == 0) from the datapath and one extra branch in the next-state logic.

Exercise 2.6. A designer proposes to implement the control unit of a simple, fast processor as a microprogram stored in a ROM, "because it can be changed later". Give one argument for and one against.

Answer

For: a ROM-based control unit can be corrected or extended by rewriting the control memory, with no redesign of logic, which suits machines with large and complicated instruction sets. Against: each step costs an extra memory read, so the machine is slower, and a simple, regular instruction set (as in RISC designs) needs little control, which hardwired logic generates directly and quickly.

docs.title: Chapter 10: From Instructions to Hardware: Datapath and Pipeline
docs.text: We now have a language for describing hardware (Chapters 3 to 7) and an instruction set to implement (Chapters 8 and 9). This chapter joins them. It shows how one RISC-V instruction is carried out by a single-cycle datapath, why that design runs at the speed of its slowest instruction, and how a five-stage pipeline overlaps instructions to keep every part of the hardware busy, at the price of hazards that forwarding and prediction have to tame. In the middle of the chapter we write a small RISC-V processor in Verilog, the capstone of the book.

docs.title: 10.1 The single-cycle datapath
docs.text:
In the single-cycle datapath each instruction runs from start to finish in one clock cycle. Its blocks are the datapath and control units of Chapter 2, now with names.

Part Job Program counter (PC) holds the address of the current instruction; moves on by 4, or is redirected by a branch or jump Instruction memory returns the 32-bit instruction at that address Register file 32 registers; reads two (rs1, rs2) and writes one (rd) per cycle Immediate generator rebuilds and sign-extends the constant hidden in the instruction ALU adds, subtracts, compares, shifts, and works out memory addresses Data memory read by loads, written by stores; its address comes from the ALU Control unit reads the opcode and function fields and sets every multiplexer and enable

Figure 10.1 shows the blocks and the main wires.

Figure 10.1. The single-cycle datapath. The control unit reads the instruction and sets the multiplexers and write enables. The branch-target adder and the next-PC multiplexer are omitted for clarity.

An instruction takes its own route through these blocks, and the control unit is what opens and closes the routes.

  • add flows PC → instruction memory → register file (read rs1 and rs2) → ALU (add) → back into the register file (write rd).
  • lw sends the ALU's address to data memory and writes the loaded value into rd.
  • sw does the same address calculation, but writes the contents of rs2 into data memory and writes no register.
  • beq uses the ALU to compare its two registers and, if they are equal, feeds the branch target back into the PC.
  • jal writes PC + 4 into rd and loads the PC with the jump target.

The control signals that select these routes, for the instructions of the machine built below, are:

Instruction reg_write alu_src (1 = immediate) mem_write mem_to_reg branch jump ALU does add, sub 1 0 0 0 0 0 add, or subtract (from funct7) addi 1 1 0 0 0 0 add lw 1 1 0 1 0 0 add (address) sw 0 1 1 – 0 0 add (address) beq 0 0 0 – 1 0 subtract (test zero) jal 1 – 0 – 0 1 none (writes PC + 4)

docs.title: 10.2 Why one instruction per cycle is slow
docs.text:
"One cycle per instruction" sounds fastest. It is not. In a single-cycle design the clock period has to be long enough for the slowest instruction, which is a load, since it walks the entire path. Every faster instruction waits for the worst case. Suppose the stages take these times (typical textbook figures, in picoseconds):

Instruction Fetch Register read ALU Memory Register write Total lw 200 100 200 200 100 800 sw 200 100 200 200 – 700 add 200 100 200 – 100 600 beq 200 100 200 – – 500

The clock period must fit the slowest, 800 ps (Figure 10.2). Every add therefore waits 200 ps that it does not need, and every beq wastes 300 ps. (One picosecond is a trillionth of a second.)

Figure 10.2. Time taken by each instruction in a single-cycle design. The clock period is set by the longest, the load.

docs.title: 10.3 A small RISC-V processor in Verilog
docs.text:
We now describe the datapath of Figure 10.1 for seven instructions: add, sub, addi, lw, sw, beq and jal. Each block is a module. The first is the register file, with the rule that x0 is always zero: writes to it are ignored, and reads of it return 0.

module regfile (
    input  wire        clk,
    input  wire        we,
    input  wire [4:0]  rs1, rs2, rd,
    input  wire [31:0] wd,
    output wire [31:0] rd1, rd2
);
    reg [31:0] x [0:31];
    integer i;
    initial for (i = 0; i < 32; i = i + 1) x[i] = 32'd0;

    always @(posedge clk)
        if (we && rd != 5'd0) x[rd] <= wd;           // x0 is never written

    assign rd1 = (rs1 == 5'd0) ? 32'd0 : x[rs1];     // x0 always reads 0
    assign rd2 = (rs2 == 5'd0) ? 32'd0 : x[rs2];
endmodule

Two read ports are combinational (the two assign statements) and one write port is clocked. The immediate generator rebuilds the constant for each format, using exactly the bit positions of Figure 8.1 and Figure 8.2, with the sign taken from bit 31:

module immgen (
    input  wire [31:0] instr,
    output reg  [31:0] imm
);
    always @(*) begin
        case (instr[6:0])
            7'b0010011, 7'b0000011:       // I-type: addi, lw
                imm = {{20{instr[31]}}, instr[31:20]};
            7'b0100011:                   // S-type: sw
                imm = {{20{instr[31]}}, instr[31:25], instr[11:7]};
            7'b1100011:                   // B-type: beq
                imm = {{19{instr[31]}}, instr[31], instr[7], instr[30:25], instr[11:8], 1'b0};
            7'b1101111:                   // J-type: jal
                imm = {{11{instr[31]}}, instr[31], instr[19:12], instr[20], instr[30:21], 1'b0};
            default: imm = 32'd0;
        endcase
    end
endmodule

The widths of the concatenations add up to 32 in each case: for example, the B-type immediate is \(19 + 1 + 1 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 32\) bits. The ALU needs only to add or subtract, and to flag a zero result for beq:

module alu32 (
    input  wire [31:0] a, b,
    input  wire        sub,
    output wire [31:0] y,
    output wire        zero
);
    assign y    = sub ? (a - b) : (a + b);
    assign zero = (y == 32'd0);
endmodule

The top level wires the blocks together and contains the control unit as one combinational case on the opcode, exactly the table above:

module mini_rv (
    input  wire        clk,
    input  wire        rst_n,
    output wire [31:0] pc_out
);
    reg  [31:0] pc;
    reg  [31:0] imem [0:63];                  // instruction memory (loaded by the testbench)
    reg  [31:0] dmem [0:63];                  // data memory

    wire [31:0] instr  = imem[pc[7:2]];       // word-aligned fetch
    wire [6:0]  opcode = instr[6:0];
    wire [4:0]  rs1 = instr[19:15], rs2 = instr[24:20], rd = instr[11:7];

    wire [31:0] imm, rd1, rd2, alu_y, alu_b, wb;
    wire        zero;

    // control unit: hardwired, one case per opcode
    reg reg_write, alu_src, mem_write, mem_to_reg, branch, jump, sub;
    always @(*) begin
        reg_write = 1'b0; alu_src = 1'b0; mem_write = 1'b0; mem_to_reg = 1'b0;
        branch    = 1'b0; jump    = 1'b0; sub       = 1'b0;
        case (opcode)
            7'b0110011: begin reg_write = 1'b1; sub = instr[30]; end              // add, sub
            7'b0010011: begin reg_write = 1'b1; alu_src = 1'b1; end               // addi
            7'b0000011: begin reg_write = 1'b1; alu_src = 1'b1; mem_to_reg = 1'b1; end  // lw
            7'b0100011: begin alu_src = 1'b1; mem_write = 1'b1; end               // sw
            7'b1100011: begin branch = 1'b1; sub = 1'b1; end                      // beq
            7'b1101111: begin reg_write = 1'b1; jump = 1'b1; end                  // jal
            default: ;
        endcase
    end

    immgen  u_imm (.instr(instr), .imm(imm));
    regfile u_rf  (.clk(clk), .we(reg_write), .rs1(rs1), .rs2(rs2), .rd(rd),
                   .wd(wb), .rd1(rd1), .rd2(rd2));
    assign alu_b = alu_src ? imm : rd2;
    alu32   u_alu (.a(rd1), .b(alu_b), .sub(sub), .y(alu_y), .zero(zero));

    wire [31:0] load_data = dmem[alu_y[7:2]];
    assign wb = jump ? (pc + 32'd4) : (mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_y);

    wire        take    = (branch & zero) | jump;
    wire [31:0] pc_next = take ? (pc + imm) : (pc + 32'd4);

    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
        if (!rst_n) pc <= 32'd0;
        else        pc <= pc_next;

    always @(posedge clk)
        if (mem_write) dmem[alu_y[7:2]] <= rd2;

    assign pc_out = pc;
endmodule

Trace one instruction through the code to see how it works. For addi t0, zero, 1 (0x00100293): the opcode is 0010011, so the control sets reg_write and alu_src; the immediate generator produces 1; the register file supplies x0 = 0; the ALU adds \(0 + 1\); wb is alu_y, the register file writes it into x5 at the clock edge, and the PC moves to PC + 4. For beq t0, t1, done, branch and sub are set, the ALU subtracts, and if the result is zero take is 1 and the PC becomes pc + imm, where imm is the branch offset.

To test it, we load the sum 1..10 program (the form with the test at the top, Section 9.4) as a list of hexadecimal words, one per line, in a file sum.hex:

00000513
00100293
00b00313
00628863
00550533
00128293
ff5ff06f
00000013

These are addi a0,zero,0; addi t0,zero,1; addi t1,zero,11; beq t0,t1,done (offset +16); add a0,a0,t0; addi t0,t0,1; jal zero,loop (offset −12); and the closing nop. The testbench runs until the PC passes the last instruction and checks the registers:

`timescale 1ns/1ps
module mini_rv_tb;
    reg  clk = 1'b0, rst_n = 1'b0;
    wire [31:0] pc;
    integer cycles = 0;

    mini_rv dut (.clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .pc_out(pc));
    always #5 clk = ~clk;
    always @(posedge clk) if (rst_n) cycles <= cycles + 1;

    initial begin
        $readmemh("sum.hex", dut.imem);
        #12 rst_n = 1'b1;
        wait (pc == 32'd32);                 // 8 instructions of 4 bytes
        #1;
        if (dut.u_rf.x[10] == 32'd55 && dut.u_rf.x[5] == 32'd11)
            $display("PASS: a0=%0d t0=%0d after %0d cycles",
                     dut.u_rf.x[10], dut.u_rf.x[5], cycles);
        else
            $display("FAIL: a0=%0d t0=%0d", dut.u_rf.x[10], dut.u_rf.x[5]);
        $finish;
    end
endmodule

On the correct design the test prints a0=55 t0=11 after 45 cycles: one instruction per cycle, and the program of Section 9.4 with the test at the top executes 45 instructions. If your count differs, trace the program by hand.

docs.title: 10.4 The five-stage pipeline
docs.text:
A pipeline splits the datapath into stages, with a register between each, so that a different instruction can be in every stage at the same time. Compare laundry. Washing, drying and folding one load at a time leaves the washer idle while you fold; start the second load washing as soon as the first has gone into the dryer, and all three machines work at once. The textbook RISC pipeline has five stages.

Stage Name What happens 1 · IF instruction fetch read the instruction at the PC; compute PC + 4 2 · ID instruction decode decode the fields, read rs1 and rs2, build the immediate 3 · EX execute the ALU computes: arithmetic, a memory address, or a branch comparison 4 · MEM memory access loads read data memory, stores write it (other instructions idle here) 5 · WB write back the result is written to rd

Figure 10.3 draws five instructions as a space-time diagram.

Figure 10.3. Five instructions overlapping in a five-stage pipeline. After the pipeline fills, one instruction completes every cycle.

Each instruction still takes five cycles from start to finish. But once the pipe is full, one finishes in every cycle. With the stage times of Section 10.2 (at most 200 ps each) the clock period can fall from 800 ps to 200 ps.

Example 10.1: how much faster?

Run \(N\) instructions on the single-cycle design (800 ps per instruction) and on an ideal five-stage pipeline (200 ps clock, no stalls).

  1. Single-cycle time: \(T_1 = 800\,N\) ps.
  2. Pipelined time: the first instruction needs 5 cycles to complete; each later one completes one cycle after the previous, so \(N\) instructions need \(N + 4\) cycles: \(T_5 = 200\,(N+4)\) ps.
  3. For \(N = 1000\): \(T_1 = 800\,000\) ps and \(T_5 = 200 \times 1004 = 200\,800\) ps.
  4. Speedup \(= 800\,000 / 200\,800 \approx 3.98\).

As \(N\) grows the speedup tends to \(800/200 = 4\), the ratio of the clock periods, and not to 5, the number of stages. The five stage times (200, 100, 200, 200 and 100 ps) are unequal, and the pipeline's clock must fit the slowest of them, so the stages cannot all be used to the full. The gain is real, but it is an ideal figure: each stall and each wrongly fetched instruction reduces it.

docs.title: 10.5 When overlapping goes wrong: hazards
docs.text: A hazard is any situation in which the next instruction cannot safely go ahead in its cycle. There are two kinds that matter here.

docs.title: Data hazards
docs.text:
add x1, x2, x3     # writes x1 in WB (cycle 5)
sub x4, x1, x5     # wants x1 in ID  (cycle 3)

The second instruction needs a result that has not been written back yet. The fix is forwarding: send the ALU's result straight to the next instruction's ALU input, without waiting for write-back (Figure 10.4a). The result of the add exists at the end of its EX stage, in cycle 3, in time for the sub to use in its own EX stage in cycle 4.

After a lw, even forwarding is one cycle too late: the loaded value exists only after the MEM stage, while an immediately following instruction wants it at the start of its EX stage. The pipeline must therefore stall for one cycle (Figure 10.4b).

Figure 10.4. Data hazards. (a) A result is forwarded from the end of EX to the next instruction's EX. (b) After a load, one stall cycle is unavoidable.

docs.title: Control hazards
docs.text:
beq t0, t1, far    # decided in EX
add ...            # already being fetched!

A branch is decided in EX, but by then the following instructions have already been fetched. Either the machine guesses (branch prediction) and throws away the wrong instructions if it guessed wrongly, or it waits. The details are the subject of the sibling book on microarchitecture.

Why RISC-V pipelines so cleanly

Fixed 32-bit instructions mean that fetch always takes the same-sized step. Register fields that never move let decode read registers at once. The load-store rule means that only the MEM stage ever touches data memory. And the few, simple formats make every stage do a short and even amount of work. The simplicity of Chapter 8 is exactly what makes a clean five-stage pipeline possible.

docs.title: 10.6 RISC-V in the world
docs.text: RISC-V is found in tiny microcontrollers and sensors, where every cent of licence fee matters; inside other chips, as management cores of SSDs, GPUs and machine-learning accelerators; in custom silicon, where companies add their own instructions for one special job; in research and in national programmes that wish to build processors without depending on a foreign licensor; and in 64-bit cores that run Linux. It is also small enough to learn completely and real enough to matter. The same encodings you have decoded by hand run on shipping chips.

docs.title: 10.7 Summary
docs.text:
• A single-cycle datapath (PC, instruction memory, register file, immediate generator, ALU, data memory, control) executes each instruction in one cycle; the control unit selects the route by setting multiplexers and write enables.
  • Its clock period must fit the slowest instruction, the load (800 ps in the example), so faster instructions waste time.
  • Each block of the datapath is a short Verilog module; the control unit is one combinational case on the opcode; the register file keeps x0 at zero.
  • A five-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB) overlaps instructions: after the fill, one instruction completes per cycle, and \(N\) instructions take \(N + 4\) cycles when nothing stalls.
  • Data hazards are solved by forwarding, except after a load, where one stall is needed; control hazards are handled by prediction or waiting.
  • RISC-V's fixed-length instructions, fixed register fields and load-store rule make the pipeline clean.

docs.title: 10.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 10.1 (capstone: a single-cycle mini RISC-V). Build the single-cycle datapath of this chapter in Verilog, supporting add, sub, addi, lw, sw, beq and jal, with modules for the PC, instruction memory (load a hex file with $readmemh), register file (x0 = 0), immediate generator, ALU (the ALU of Chapter 5 widened to 32 bits) and data memory, and a control unit. Assemble the sum 1..10 program to hex, load it and run it. The testbench stops when the PC passes the last instruction and checks the registers. What should the registers and the cycle count be? Bonus: add bne, slt and andi and run the programs of Exercise 9.4.

Answer

The modules of Section 10.3 are one solution. After the sum 1..10 program, a0 (x10) holds 55 and t0 (x5) holds 11. The version with the branch at the top takes 45 cycles at one instruction per cycle (the version with the test at the bottom takes 33). Compare your cycle count with the pipelined machine of Section 10.4: the pipeline would take the same 45 instructions plus 4 cycles of fill (49 cycles, ignoring the stalls caused by the taken branches), but each cycle would be four times shorter. For the bonus, bne needs only the funct3 bit that selects "not equal" in the branch test; slt and andi need the ALU to gain a compare and an AND, which the control selects from funct3.

Exercise 10.2. Using the stage times of Section 10.2, what is the minimum clock period of a single-cycle machine that executes only add, sw and beq? And of one that executes lw as well? By what factor is the second slower?

Answer

Without lw the slowest instruction is sw at 700 ps, so the period is 700 ps. With lw the period must be 800 ps. The second machine is slower by \(800/700 \approx 1.14\), about 14%, on every instruction, including those that never touch memory.

Exercise 10.3. A program of 100 instructions runs on the ideal five-stage pipeline of Section 10.4. How many cycles does it take with no stalls? How many with 10 load-use stalls? How long does it take in nanoseconds at 200 ps per cycle?

Answer

With no stalls it takes \(100 + 4 = 104\) cycles. Each load-use stall adds one cycle, so 10 stalls give \(114\) cycles. At 200 ps (0.2 ns) per cycle, the second case takes \(114 \times 0.2 = 22.8\) ns.

Exercise 10.4. Identify the data hazards in this sequence and say which need a stall with forwarding.

lw  t0, 0(a0)
add t1, t0, t2
add t3, t1, t0
sub t4, t3, t1
Answer

Instruction 2 reads t0 right after the load that writes it: a load-use hazard, which needs one stall even with forwarding. Instruction 3 reads t1 from instruction 2 (the previous instruction, forwarded from EX) and t0 from instruction 1 (two instructions earlier, available from the MEM/WB stage by the time it is needed): no stall. Instruction 4 reads t3 from instruction 3 (forwarded from EX) and t1 from instruction 2 (two earlier): no stall. In total there is one stall, so the four instructions take \(4 + 4 + 1 = 9\) cycles.

Exercise 10.5. For the single-cycle machine, which control signals are 1 for lw, and which route does the loaded value take to the register file? Why is reg_write 0 for sw?

Answer

For lw, reg_write, alu_src and mem_to_reg are 1: the ALU adds the base register and the immediate to form the address, alu_src selects the immediate as the second ALU input, the address goes to data memory, and mem_to_reg selects the loaded data (rather than the ALU result) as the write-back value for rd. sw writes memory and no register, so reg_write is 0 and mem_write is 1; it also needs alu_src = 1 for the address, and the value stored is rs2.

Exercise 10.6. Explain in two sentences why a pipeline does not make any single instruction finish sooner, yet makes a program finish sooner.

Answer

Each instruction still passes through all five stages, so its own latency is five cycles (and, with the shorter clock, no shorter than before). But the stages work on different instructions at the same time, so after the pipeline fills, one instruction completes in every cycle, which increases throughput, the number of instructions finished per unit time, and so shortens the whole program.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: ABI (application binary interface) The convention that gives each register a role and says which registers a called function must preserve, so that code written by different people works together. A convention, not hardware. Active low A signal that does its job when it is 0. By convention its name ends in _n, as in rst_n. ALU (arithmetic logic unit) The combinational block that performs the arithmetic and logic microoperations; in a processor it also computes memory addresses and compares values for branches. Architecture (VHDL) The inside of a design unit: the concurrent statements and processes that implement an entity. Assertion A VHDL statement (assert ... report ... severity) that checks a condition during simulation and reports when it is false. Asynchronous reset A reset that acts the instant it is asserted, without waiting for a clock edge. In Verilog and VHDL it appears in the sensitivity list of the clocked process. Behavioural description A description of what a circuit does, without saying how it is built; also the style of coding in an always block or a process, from which synthesis works out the gates. Blocking assignment The Verilog assignment =, which takes effect immediately and in order. Used for combinational logic. Branch prediction A guess, made by a pipeline, of the outcome of a branch before it is decided, so that fetching can go on; wrongly fetched instructions are discarded. Bus One set of shared wires carrying the value of exactly one chosen register at a time. Callee-saved register A register (s0–s11, sp in RISC-V) that a function must leave unchanged when it returns, saving and restoring it if it uses it. Caller-saved register A register (t0–t6, a0–a7, ra) that a called function may overwrite; the caller must save it first if it needs the value afterwards. Clock edge The instant at which the clock changes, usually 0 to 1 (the rising edge). Registers load only at clock edges. Combinational logic Logic whose outputs depend only on the present inputs, with no memory. Concatenation Joining bits side by side into a wider vector: {a, b} in Verilog, a & b in VHDL. It builds no logic, only wiring. Control function The Boolean condition before the colon in a conditional transfer, such as P in P: R2 ← R1. Control unit The finite state machine that asserts the control signals of the datapath in the right order. Datapath The registers, ALU, shifters, buses and multiplexers where data is held and transformed. DUT (device under test) The design that a testbench instantiates and drives. Entity (VHDL) The interface of a design unit: its name and its ports. Enumerated type A VHDL type whose values are names, used for the states of a state machine. Finite state machine (FSM) A circuit that is always in one of a finite number of states and moves between them on clock edges. The control unit of an RTL design is an FSM. Forwarding Sending a result directly from a pipeline stage to the ALU input of a later instruction, without waiting for it to be written to the register file. funct3, funct7 Fields of a RISC-V instruction that, together with the opcode, select the operation. Generate A construct (Verilog generate, VHDL for ... generate) that builds repeated structure while the design is being elaborated. Generic / parameter A constant chosen when a design is instantiated, such as a bit width: generic in VHDL, parameter in Verilog. Hardwired control A control unit built from gates and a state register, fast but fixed. Hazard A situation in a pipeline in which the next instruction cannot safely go ahead in its cycle: a data hazard, or a control hazard. High impedance (Z) The state of an output that is not driving its wire at all. Immediate A constant held in the instruction itself. In RISC-V it is sign-extended to 32 bits. Instruction set architecture (ISA) The specification of the instructions a processor understands, its registers, its memory addressing and the encoding of the instructions. Latch A level-sensitive storage element. In a hardware description it is usually an accident, caused by a combinational block that does not assign an output on every path. Leaf function A function that calls no other function, and so need not save ra. Load-store architecture An architecture in which only load and store instructions access memory, and arithmetic works on registers alone. Mealy machine A state machine whose outputs depend on the state and on the inputs. Microoperation An elementary operation on register contents, completed in one clock pulse. Microprogrammed control A control unit that reads its control signals from a small memory, one word per step. Flexible, but slower. Module The building block of Verilog: a name, ports and a body. Moore machine A state machine whose outputs depend on the state only. Non-blocking assignment The Verilog assignment <=, which reads all right-hand sides first and updates all left-hand sides together at the end of the time step. Used for clocked logic; the counterpart of the RTL arrow. numeric_std The IEEE VHDL package that defines unsigned and signed vectors and their arithmetic and conversions. Opcode The low 7 bits of a RISC-V instruction, which identify its format and class. Pipeline A datapath divided into stages so that several instructions are in progress at once. Process (VHDL) A concurrent statement that contains sequential statements, used for combinational and clocked logic. Pseudo-instruction An assembler shorthand, such as li, mv, nop, j or ret, that expands to one or more real instructions. Register A group of flip-flops that holds a multi-bit value until it is told to load a new one. Register file The array of registers of a processor, with read ports and a write port. Register transfer level (RTL) The level of description of a synchronous circuit as data moving between registers under a clock, with operations and control. RISC and CISC Reduced and complex instruction set computers: few, simple, regular instructions against many powerful instructions of varying length. Sensitivity list The signals whose changes make an always block or a process run again. Sign extension Copying the top bit of a narrow signed value leftwards to fill a wider one, which preserves its value. Signal (VHDL) A wire or register between blocks, updated when the process that assigns it suspends. Stack A region of memory used to save values across function calls; in RISC-V it grows downwards and sp points at its top. std_logic The IEEE nine-valued VHDL logic type, which models drivers, high impedance and unknowns. Synthesis Turning a hardware description into a netlist of gates and flip-flops. Testbench A design unit with no ports that drives a design under test and checks its outputs. Never synthesised. Trace table A table with a row per step and a column per register of interest, used to predict and check the behaviour of a program or circuit. Tri-state An output that can be driven to 0, to 1 or left undriven (high impedance), so that several drivers can share a bus. Variable (VHDL) Local storage inside a process, updated immediately. wire and reg (Verilog) A wire is driven continuously; a reg is assigned in a procedural block. A reg is not necessarily a register. x (unknown) A Verilog logic value meaning unknown: an unset register, or two drivers in conflict. x0 (RISC-V) The register that is hard-wired to zero: reads give 0 and writes are ignored.

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
The following are the standards and the standard texts on which a reader can build. They are listed by title so that you can find the current edition.

Standards and specifications

  • IEEE Standard for Verilog Hardware Description Language (IEEE 1364), and IEEE Standard for SystemVerilog (IEEE 1800), which includes it.
  • IEEE Standard for VHDL Language Reference Manual (IEEE 1076), with its companion packages std_logic_1164 and numeric_std.
  • The RISC-V Instruction Set Manual, Volume I: Unprivileged ISA, published by RISC-V International. It defines RV32I, the extensions and the instruction encodings used in Chapters 8 to 10.

Books

  • M. Morris Mano, Computer System Architecture and Digital Design. The register-transfer notation used in Chapters 1 and 2 is the notation of these texts.
  • David A. Patterson and John L. Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design: The Hardware/Software Interface, RISC-V edition. The source of the single-cycle datapath and the five-stage pipeline of Chapter 10, with much more on hazards.
  • Sarah L. Harris and David Harris, Digital Design and Computer Architecture, which develops digital design in both Verilog and VHDL and ends with a processor.

Free tools

  • Icarus Verilog (iverilog, vvp) and Verilator, for simulating Verilog; GTKWave, for viewing waveforms; GHDL, for simulating VHDL.
  • Yosys, an open-source synthesis tool that shows what hardware a description produces.
  • EDA Playground, a browser-based environment that runs Icarus Verilog and GHDL with nothing to install.

Where to go next

With a correct RTL description in hand, two directions open. One turns the instruction set into a fast core, with pipelining, out-of-order execution, caches, on-chip interconnect and the interfaces (UART, SPI, I²C) that connect a processor to the world; the first sibling book in this collection follows it. The other follows the description through synthesis, floorplanning, placement, clock-tree synthesis, routing and timing signoff until it becomes a layout ready for manufacture; the second sibling book follows that.

docs.title: Who this book is for
docs.text:
Nobody draws a modern processor gate by gate. A chip with billions of transistors is described in text, simulated until the designers believe it works, and only then handed to tools that turn the description into gates, wires and finally silicon. The skill of writing that description is the subject of this book. It starts from the idea that makes the whole practice possible, the register transfer level (RTL), then teaches the two industrial hardware description languages, Verilog and VHDL, side by side, and ends with the open RISC-V instruction set, which is small enough to understand completely and real enough to run in shipping products.

The book is written for students of computer architecture, digital design and embedded systems. It assumes that you already know logic gates, flip-flops, binary numbers and two's complement arithmetic, and nothing more. No earlier programming in a hardware language is needed. If you have written software, one habit will have to be put aside very early: in hardware, everything happens at once. Many of the mistakes that beginners make come from reading hardware descriptions as if they were programs, and the early chapters return to this point again and again.

docs.title: What is in the book
docs.text:
The chapters follow a single line of thought, from the abstraction to the language to a complete machine.

Chapters Topic What you will be able to do 1 and 2 Register transfer level: registers, the clock, microoperations, buses, memory, datapath and control Read and write register-transfer statements, and turn a small specification into a table of microoperations and a control schedule 3, 4 and 5 Verilog: modules, signals, combinational and sequential logic, state machines, an adder and an ALU, testbenches Write synthesizable Verilog for common blocks and prove it correct with a self-checking testbench 6 and 7 VHDL: entities, architectures, processes, numeric types, generics, testbenches Write the same designs in VHDL and translate between the two languages 8, 9 and 10 RISC-V: the instruction formats, assembly programming and tracing, the single-cycle datapath and the five-stage pipeline Encode and decode instructions, trace programs by hand, and build a small RISC-V processor Back matter Glossary and further reading Look up a term, and find where to read more

The material was developed as a six-part course (register transfers, Verilog, VHDL, the RISC-V architecture, a hands-on RISC-V session and a set of ten assignments). In this book the lectures and the written notes of that course are merged into a single running text, the interactive demonstrations of the course are replaced by traces, tables and figures that you can follow on paper, and the ten assignments appear as exercises at the end of the chapters where their topics are taught. Answers are folded under each exercise; the phrase "Answer" opens one when you want it.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
Read with a pencil. Hardware cannot be learned by looking at code: it has to be predicted, run and compared. The method used throughout, and the one that the exercises ask you to follow, is predict first, then check. Before you read the result of a worked example, work out for yourself what each register will hold after each clock edge, and write it in a trace table. A prediction that can turn out wrong is the only thing that tells you whether you understand.

You will also want to run the code. All the tools you need are free:

  • Icarus Verilog (iverilog, vvp) simulates Verilog, and GTKWave shows the waveforms it records.
  • GHDL simulates VHDL.
  • EDA Playground, in a web browser, runs Icarus Verilog and GHDL with nothing to set up.
  • Yosys is an open-source synthesis tool; it shows what hardware a description really produces.

A typical session is iverilog -g2012 -o sim design.v design_tb.v followed by vvp sim, for Verilog, and ghdl -a design.vhd design_tb.vhd, ghdl -e design_tb, ghdl -r design_tb --vcd=wave.vcd, for VHDL. The listings are written to be read as well as run, so treat them as models of style, and type them in rather than pasting them where you can.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text: Worked examples sit in boxes headed "Example", definitions in note boxes and common mistakes in warning boxes. Code is set in fixed-width type with the language named. A signal or register whose name ends in _n (for example rst_n) is active low: it does its job when it is 0. Numbers written in Verilog style, such as 8'hA5, give a width, a base and the digits; 0x introduces hexadecimal in assembly language and in prose. Register-transfer statements are written with the arrow of Morris Mano's notation, R2 ← R1; the code listings use the ASCII <= that the languages themselves use.

docs.title: A note on the two languages
docs.text:
Verilog and VHDL are two spellings of the same ideas. Verilog (standardised as IEEE 1364, and now part of SystemVerilog, IEEE 1800) is terse and permissive. VHDL (IEEE 1076) is verbose and strict, and reads like a contract. Both are used in industry, and a working engineer is expected to read both. The book teaches Verilog first, because its brevity lets the central ideas show clearly, and then shows how every one of those ideas is written in VHDL. Chapter 7 closes with a table that translates the constructs one by one.

The two sibling books of this collection continue the story. The first turns the instruction set into a fast core, with pipelining, caches and on-chip interconnect. The second follows an RTL description through synthesis, placement, routing and signoff until it becomes the layout of a chip. This book ends exactly where the hardware description is complete and correct.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Registers, the Clock and Microoperations
docs.text: This chapter introduces the abstraction on which the rest of the book depends. It explains why designers describe hardware as data moving between registers, defines the vocabulary (register, clock, microoperation, control function), shows the four families of microoperations, and ends with a complete small design, a 4-bit counter, taken from a specification to a table of microoperations to working code. After it you will be able to read and write statements such as P: R2 ← R1, and to say exactly what they mean for the hardware.

docs.title: 1.1 Why describe hardware at all?
docs.text:
A modern processor contains billions of transistors, and nobody draws them. Instead, designers write a description of the machine, in text, and rely on software to turn the description into a circuit. The question is what the description should say.

Think of a chip as a small factory. Registers are the shelves: small boxes of flip-flops, each holding one number. Combinational logic is the workstations (adders, comparators, multiplexers), which compute but remember nothing. The clock is the factory whistle: at each tick, every shelf takes in its new contents at the same moment. Control is the foreman, who decides which shelf receives what on each tick.

There are three useful ways to describe the same machine. Suppose we want a circuit that finds the greatest common divisor of two numbers \(A\) and \(B\).

  • The behavioural description is gcd(A, B). It says what the answer is and nothing about hardware, so nothing can be built from it directly.
  • The gate-level description is a netlist of AND gates, OR gates, inverters and flip-flops, perhaps three thousand of them, with every wire named. It is exact, but it is far too detailed for a person to reason about.
  • The register-transfer description says which registers exist, what is computed from them, and when each one changes:
while A != B:
    if A > B:  A <- A - B
    else:      B <- B - A

The third level is the register transfer level, or RTL. It sits deliberately between the other two.

Figure 1.1. The three levels of description of the same machine: behaviour, register transfers and gates.

Definition: Register Transfer Level

Register Transfer Level (RTL) is a design abstraction that models a synchronous digital circuit as the flow of data between registers, and the logical operations performed on that data, all sequenced by a clock. An RTL description names three things and nothing more: the registers (memory is just a large array of registers), the operations performed on their contents, and the control that decides which operations happen and in what order.

Designers work at this level for two reasons. First, it is the level that a synthesis tool reads: a program that turns an RTL description into a netlist of gates and flip-flops automatically. You write what should move where and when, and the tool works out the gates. Second, it is still small enough for a person to read and to convince themselves that it is correct. You can look at a datapath and a sequence of control steps and see that the machine does the right thing.

An everyday comparison may help. Imagine giving a friend directions to your house. "Come to my house" is too vague to follow (behaviour). "Take bus 12, get off at the third stop and walk 200 m north" is exact enough to follow and short enough to check (RTL). "Lift your left foot 4 cm, move it 70 cm forward, put it down..." is correct, but no one could check it (gates). The middle version names places, moves and moments, which are exactly the registers, the operations and the clock ticks that RTL names.

RTL is a level, not a language

RTL is a level of description, independent of any language. The notation of this chapter is the register-transfer notation of Morris Mano's computer-organisation texts, and it needs no hardware language at all. Verilog and VHDL are languages in which an RTL description can be written down so that machines can read it. The same languages can also express things that are not RTL, such as delays and file input, and those cannot be synthesized.

docs.title: 1.2 Registers and the clock
docs.text:
A register is a group of flip-flops that stores a multi-bit value until it is told to load a new one. A register is given a short symbolic name: R1, R2, or a name that says what it is for, such as PC (the program counter, which holds the address of the next instruction), AR (the address register) or ACC (the accumulator, in which results build up). Its bits are numbered from 0 at the right.

Everything in a synchronous system is paced by the clock. The instant at which the clock rises from 0 to 1 is the rising edge, and on that instant every register that is enabled loads its new value simultaneously. Between edges, the combinational logic in front of each register is still working out the next value; it settles well before the next edge, and the register ignores it until then.

The consequence is the rule that makes digital hardware predictable: a register changes only on clock edges, never in between. A "transfer" is therefore not a gradual thing. It happens atomically, at one edge.

docs.title: 1.3 Microoperations
docs.text:
A microoperation is an elementary operation on the contents of registers that completes in a single clock pulse. The fundamental one is the register transfer, written with an arrow:

R2 <- R1        at the next clock edge, R2 receives a copy of R1

R1 is not changed: a transfer copies, it does not move.

docs.title: Conditional transfers
docs.text:
Most transfers must not happen on every clock edge. A Boolean condition written before a colon, called a control function, says when:

P: R2 <- R1     if P = 1 at the edge, R2 gets R1;  if P = 0, R2 keeps its value

In hardware, P drives the load input of R2. Figure 1.2 shows the timing. The signal P is high around the third edge, so R2 loads R1 (here 5) at that edge and not at the others.

Figure 1.2. Timing of the conditional transfer P: R2 ← R1. R2 changes only just after the edge at which P is 1.

docs.title: Simultaneous transfers
docs.text:
Several transfers can be listed together, separated by commas. A comma means "in the same clock pulse":

T3: R1 <- R2, R2 <- R1

All the right-hand sides are read first, from the old values; then every left-hand side is written at the edge. That is why this single line swaps two registers: no temporary register is needed.

Example 1.1: the swap in one clock pulse

Let \(R1 = 5\) and \(R2 = 9\), and let T: R1 ← R2, R2 ← R1.

  1. With T = 1, at the edge both right-hand sides are sampled: R2 supplies 9 and R1 supplies 5.
  2. Both registers then load at once: R1 takes 9 and R2 takes 5.
  3. Result: R1 = 9, R2 = 5. A clean swap.
  4. With T = 0 nothing loads and the registers stay at R1 = 5, R2 = 9.

Had the first transfer taken effect before the second one read its source, R1 would hold 9 when R2 ← R1 was evaluated, and both registers would end at 9. This is the single most common misunderstanding of RTL, and it is the reason hardware languages distinguish two kinds of assignment (Chapter 3).

docs.title: The four families
docs.text:
Every microoperation belongs to one of four families, and every datapath you will meet is assembled from them.

Family What it does Symbols Example Transfer copies data unchanged ← R2 ← R1 Arithmetic add, subtract, increment, decrement, complement + − R+1 R3 ← R1 + R2 Logic bit-by-bit Boolean operations ∧ ∨ ⊕ and a bar for complement R1 ← R1 ⊕ R2 Shift moves bits left or right shl shr cil cir R1 ← shl R1

Here ∧ is AND, ∨ is OR, ⊕ is exclusive-OR, and a bar over a name means the bitwise complement. The operations shl and shr shift left and right, filling with 0, while cil and cir rotate (circular shift left and right), so that the bit that falls off one end re-enters at the other.

Example 1.2: four microoperations on the same registers

Start every line from \(R1 = 0110\) (6) and \(R2 = 0011\) (3).

Microoperation Working Result R3 ← R1 + R2 0110 + 0011 1001 (9) R1 ← R1 ⊕ R2 0110 ⊕ 0011, a 1 wherever the bits differ 0101 R1 ← shl R1 0110 moves one place left, a 0 enters at the right 1100 (12 = 6 × 2) R2 ← R2 complemented every bit of 0011 flips 1100

A left shift doubles a number. Hardware uses this everywhere, because a shift is only wiring, and wiring is far cheaper than a multiplier.

docs.title: Subtraction needs no subtractor
docs.text:
Subtracting is the same as adding the two's complement: \(R1 - R2 = R1 + \overline{R2} + 1\). An ALU that can add and complement can therefore also subtract, and the carry-in of the adder supplies the "+ 1" at no cost.

Example 1.3: 6 − 3 with an adder

With \(R1 = 0110\) and \(R2 = 0011\):

  R1         0110      6
  not R2     1100      complement of 0011
  + 1           1
  ------------------
            1 0011     keep 4 bits: 0011 = 3

The carry out of the top (the leading 1) is discarded. Spotting reuse like this is the first payoff of thinking in RTL: one adder, several operations.

docs.title: 1.4 Common misconceptions
docs.text:
Three beliefs trip up almost everyone at first.

Misconception: the arrows run in order, like a program

No. Transfers in one pulse happen together: all old values are read, then all registers load at the edge. That is why R1 ← R2, R2 ← R1 swaps. Treating register transfers as sequential program statements is the most common RTL error.

Misconception: RTL is just a coding style

No. It is a level of description. You can write RTL on paper with no language, and you can write Verilog that is not RTL at all (with delays such as #10, which have no meaning in silicon).

Misconception: the adder works for the whole cycle

No. In R3 ← R1 + R2 the addition is combinational and settles quickly. The register is the timed element: the clock edge decides when the answer is captured, not how long the adder works.

docs.title: 1.5 A worked design: a 4-bit counter
docs.text:
We now take a small machine from specification to hardware. We want a 4-bit register \(Q\) that counts up. It has two control inputs: clr clears \(Q\) and has priority, and en lets the register count. There is exactly one datapath register (\(Q\)) and two control signals, so the whole design is captured by a short table of conditional transfers.

When Control function Microoperation Effect Clear clr Q ← 0000 back to zero Count clr'·en Q ← Q + 1 up by one; 1111 wraps to 0000 Hold clr'·en' Q ← Q unchanged

(A prime marks a complemented control signal: clr' is "clr is 0".) The hold row needs no hardware, because a register that is not told to load simply keeps its value. The design is therefore two conditional transfers.

Figure 1.3 traces the counter edge by edge. Each edge sees the values of en and clr that were present just before it. At the first four edges en = 1 and clr = 0, so \(Q\) counts 0001, 0010, 0011, 0100. For the next two edges en = 0, so \(Q\) holds 0100. Then en returns and \(Q\) counts to 0101; at the next edge clr is 1, and although en is also 1, the clear wins and \(Q\) jumps to 0000.

Figure 1.3. The counter traced edge by edge. Q changes only just after a clock edge, and clr overrides en.

The table translates into Verilog line for line. The language is taught in Chapters 3 to 5; for now, simply look for the shared shape: one row of the table, one line of code.

always @(posedge clk) begin
    if (clr)        Q <= 4'b0000;   // clr:        Q <- 0000
    else if (en)    Q <= Q + 1;     // clr' & en:  Q <- Q + 1
    // otherwise Q holds its value by itself
end

The condition clr is tested first, so it wins, which is exactly the priority that the specification asked for. Reversing the order of the two tests would give en priority over clr, a different machine.

docs.title: 1.6 Summary
docs.text:
• RTL describes a clocked circuit as registers + operations + clock + control. It lies between vague behaviour and unreadable gates, and it is the level that synthesis tools read.
  • The unit of work is the microoperation, written P: R2 ← R1: a conditional transfer completed in one clock pulse.
  • Microoperations come in four families: transfer, arithmetic, logic and shift. Subtraction is addition of the complement.
  • Transfers in one pulse are simultaneous: every right-hand side is read from the old values before any register changes.
  • A register changes only at clock edges. The clock edge decides when a result is captured; the combinational logic only has to settle before it.
  • A small machine can be specified completely by a table of control functions and microoperations, and the table maps directly to code.

docs.title: 1.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1.1 (register transfers on paper). Registers are R1 = 5 and R2 = 9, and P is a 1-bit flag. The microoperations are P: R1 ← R2, R2 ← R1 and P': R1 ← R1 + R2. For each value of P, give the contents of R1 and R2 after one clock edge. Explain why the swap needs no temporary register, and what would go wrong if the two transfers were executed one after the other as in a program.

Answer P Microoperation that fires R1 after the edge R2 after the edge 1 R1 ← R2, R2 ← R1 9 5 0 R1 ← R1 + R2 14 9

Both registers sample their inputs at the same edge, so each takes the other's old value and no temporary register is needed. Executed one after the other, the first transfer would change R1 before the second one read it, so R2 would receive the new R1 (that is, 9), and both registers would end up equal to 9.

Exercise 1.2. Start from R1 = 0110 and R2 = 0011. Give the result of each of these microoperations: R3 ← R1 ∧ R2; R3 ← R1 ∨ R2; R1 ← cil R1; R2 ← cir R2.

Answer

AND is 1 only where both bits are 1: 0110 ∧ 0011 = 0010. OR is 1 where either bit is 1: 0110 ∨ 0011 = 0111. Rotating 0110 left by one place moves the top bit (0) to the right end: 1100. Rotating 0011 right by one place moves the low bit (1) to the top: 1001.

Exercise 1.3. Compute 9 − 4 on 4-bit registers using only addition and complement. What does the carry out of the top bit tell you?

Answer

\(9 = 1001\) and \(4 = 0100\), so \(\overline{4} = 1011\). Then \(1001 + 1011 + 1 = 10101\). Keeping four bits gives \(0101 = 5\). The carry out of the top bit is 1, which means that no borrow was needed (\(9 \ge 4\)). If the carry were 0, the first operand would have been smaller than the second.

Exercise 1.4. Four 8-bit registers are to be connected so that any register can be copied into any other. (a) How many one-way paths and how many wires are needed if every pair is wired directly? (b) How many data wires does a single bus need? What else does the bus need?

Answer

(a) With \(n = 4\) registers there are \(n(n-1) = 12\) one-way paths; each carries 8 bits, so \(12 \times 8 = 96\) wires. (b) A bus needs only 8 data wires, shared by all registers. It needs, in addition, a way to choose which register drives it (select lines for a multiplexer, or enables for tri-state buffers) and a load signal for each destination register. Chapter 2 develops this.

Exercise 1.5. The counter of Section 1.5 holds Q = 1110. On the next three clock edges the inputs are (clr, en) = (0,1), (0,1), (1,1). What is Q after each edge?

Answer

After the first edge Q = 1111. After the second edge it wraps: Q = 0000. At the third edge clr = 1, and clear has priority over count, so Q = 0000 again.

docs.title: Chapter 9: RISC-V Assembly Programming and Tracing
docs.text:
Knowing the formats is not yet knowing the machine. This chapter runs real RISC-V programs, on paper, one instruction at a time. It teaches a method (predict first, then step, and keep a trace table) and applies it to arithmetic and logic, memory, loops, decisions, a Fibonacci calculation, a function call that uses the stack, and a recursive function. By the end you should be able to predict what a short RISC-V program leaves in each register, and the number of instructions it takes to do so, and to find the classic bugs by reading the last row of a trace.

All the programs here are written in RV32I assembly. In the course on which this book is based, they were run in a small simulator that shows the 32 registers, the data memory and the 32 bits of the current instruction, and every result below is the one that simulator produced. The simulator assumes that sp starts at 1024 and that memory is empty; the traces here use the same convention. Any RV32I simulator will do for your own runs.

docs.title: 9.1 Predict, then step
docs.text:
The method has four steps.

  1. Read the next instruction.
  2. Predict which register changes, and to what value. Say it aloud or write it down.
  3. Step, that is, carry out the instruction, and compare.
  4. If you were wrong, find out why before going on. That moment is where the learning happens.

Watching numbers change feels like understanding, but it is not. Only a prediction that can turn out wrong tells you whether you really know what an instruction does. To keep score, use a trace table: one row per step, and one column for each register that matters. Several are filled in below.

docs.title: 9.2 Arithmetic and logic
docs.text:
Eight instructions, eight predictions. Suppose t0 = 12 and t1 = 5:

addi t0, zero, 12   # t0 = 12
addi t1, zero, 5    # t1 = 5
add  t2, t0, t1     # t2 = ?
sub  t3, t0, t1     # t3 = ?
and  t4, t0, t1     # t4 = ?
or   t5, t0, t1     # t5 = ?
xor  t6, t0, t1     # t6 = ?
slli a0, t0, 2      # a0 = ?

Write your six answers down before reading on. The logic instructions work bit by bit, so write the numbers in binary first: \(12 = 1100\) and \(5 = 0101\).

  1100        1100        1100
& 0101      | 0101      ^ 0101
  ----        ----        ----
  0100 = 4    1101 = 13   1001 = 9

The rest follow: add gives \(12 + 5 = 17\), sub gives \(12 - 5 = 7\), and slli shifts \(1100\) left by two places, appending two 0 bits, to give \(110000 = 48\), which is multiplication by \(2^2 = 4\).

Register t2 t3 t4 t5 t6 a0 Value 17 7 4 13 9 48

docs.title: 9.3 Memory: loads and stores
docs.text:
Only two kinds of instruction may touch memory, and they must do it with a register as the base address. RISC-V uses byte addressing: each address names one byte (8 bits). A register holds 32 bits, which is 4 bytes, so a word stored at address 100 fills bytes 100, 101, 102 and 103, and the next word starts at 104, not 101. Arrays of words therefore step by 4, and sw t1, 4(t0) means "the word after the one at t0".

Example 9.1: stores and loads

Predict what ends up in a0, a1 and a2.

addi t0, zero, 100   # base address
addi t1, zero, 42
sw   t1, 0(t0)       # M[100] = 42
addi t1, zero, 7
sw   t1, 4(t0)       # M[104] = 7
lw   a0, 0(t0)       # a0 = M[100]
lw   a1, 4(t0)       # a1 = M[104]
add  a2, a0, a1      # a2 = a0 + a1
  1. t0 holds 100, the base address. t1 first holds 42.
  2. sw t1, 0(t0) copies 42 into the word at address 100.
  3. t1 is reused: it becomes 7. This does not change memory, because the store copied the value and nothing reaches back.
  4. sw t1, 4(t0) copies 7 into the word at address \(100 + 4 = 104\).
  5. The loads read them back: a0 = 42 and a1 = 7. Finally a2 = 42 + 7 = 49.

Figure 9.1 shows what memory holds. RISC-V stores the least significant byte of a word at the lowest address (it is little-endian), so the word 42 (0x2A) puts 2A at address 100 and zeros at 101 to 103.

Figure 9.1. Byte addresses 100 to 107 after the two stores. Each word occupies four bytes; the second word starts at 104.

docs.title: 9.4 Loops and decisions
docs.text:
A loop is a counter, an accumulator and a conditional branch back. The program below sums \(1 + 2 + \dots + 10\) and tests at the bottom of the loop.

    addi a0, zero, 0      # a0 = 0   (running total)
    addi t0, zero, 1      # t0 = 1   (counter i)
    addi t1, zero, 11     # t1 = 11  (limit: stop when i == 11)
loop:
    add  a0, a0, t0       # a0 = a0 + i
    addi t0, t0, 1        # i = i + 1
    bne  t0, t1, loop     # if i != 11, go again

Example 9.2: a trace table for 1 + 2 + … + 10

After each pass of the loop (add, addi, bne):

Pass t0 (i) after addi a0 after add bne result 1 2 1 taken (2 ≠ 11) 2 3 3 taken 3 4 6 taken 4 5 10 taken 5 6 15 taken ⋮ ⋮ ⋮ ⋮ 9 10 45 taken 10 11 55 not taken: falls out

The accumulator after pass \(k\) is \(k(k+1)/2\), and it reaches 55 on pass 10. There are 3 set-up instructions and 10 passes of 3 instructions each, so the program executes \(3 + 10 \times 3 = 33\) instructions.

docs.title: Testing at the top
docs.text:
The same sum can be written with the test at the top of the loop, as many beginners would write it:

    addi a0, zero, 0      # sum = 0
    addi t0, zero, 1      # i = 1
    addi t1, zero, 11     # limit = 11
loop:
    beq  t0, t1, done     # if i == 11, leave
    add  a0, a0, t0       # sum += i
    addi t0, t0, 1        # i++
    jal  zero, loop       # go round again
done:
    nop                   # result is in a0

The trace is the same except that beq is evaluated first, so a table of the values seen at beq is: first t0 = 1, a0 = 0; second t0 = 2, a0 = 1; third t0 = 3, a0 = 3; and so on to the tenth, t0 = 10, a0 = 45; the eleventh test sees t0 = 11, a0 = 55, and leaves.

Layout Instructions per pass Total Test at the top 4 (beq, add, addi, jal) \(3 + 10 \times 4 + 1 + 1 = 45\) Test at the bottom 3 (add, addi, bne) \(3 + 10 \times 3 = 33\)

The first total counts the three set-up instructions, ten passes of four, the last beq that leaves, and the nop. The bottom-test form needs no jump back and runs about a quarter fewer instructions for the same answer. Compilers turn loops "upside down" like this all the time.

docs.title: The classic loop bug
docs.text:
What if the limit register had been loaded with 10 instead of 11?

    addi t1, zero, 10     # limit = 10  (the change)

The loop leaves when i reaches 10, before adding 10, so the answer becomes \(1 + 2 + \dots + 9 = 45\), not 55. Stopping one pass too early or too late is an off-by-one error, the commonest loop bug in every language. A trace table catches it: look at the last row.

docs.title: A decision
docs.text:
A high-level if (t0 < t1) a0 = 1; else a0 = 2; becomes a compare-and-branch:

    blt  t0, t1, then     # condition true? jump to the then part
    addi a0, zero, 2      # else part
    jal  zero, done       # jump over the then part
then:
    addi a0, zero, 1      # then part
done:

The branch jumps when the condition is true. If it falls through, the else part runs and then jumps over the then part. Exactly one of the two addi instructions runs, and every if/else in every language compiles to this shape.

docs.title: 9.5 Fibonacci: two values moving together
docs.text:
Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the two before it. The program keeps \(a\) in t0 and \(b\) in t1, two neighbours in the list, and slides them one place along on every pass:

    addi t0, zero, 0      # a = 0
    addi t1, zero, 1      # b = 1
    addi t2, zero, 10     # count = 10
loop:
    beq  t2, zero, done
    add  t3, t0, t1       # t3 = a + b
    add  t0, zero, t1     # a = b
    add  t1, zero, t3     # b = a + b
    addi t2, t2, -1       # count down
    jal  zero, loop
done:
    add  a0, zero, t0     # result in a0

t3 is a temporary: without it, the new b would overwrite the old one before it could be copied into a.

Example 9.3: trace of the Fibonacci loop

The table shows the registers when beq is evaluated, at the start of each pass.

Test t2 (count) t0 (a) t1 (b) start 10 0 1 after pass 1 9 1 1 after pass 2 8 1 2 after pass 3 7 2 3 after pass 4 6 3 5 after pass 5 5 5 8 after pass 6 4 8 13 after pass 7 3 13 21 after pass 8 2 21 34 after pass 9 1 34 55 after pass 10 0 55 89

When t2 reaches 0, beq jumps to done, and a0 = t0 = 55, the tenth Fibonacci number (\(F_{10} = 55\), with \(F_0 = 0\) and \(F_1 = 1\)). The instruction count is 3 for set-up, 6 per pass for ten passes, the final beq and the closing add: \(3 + 6 \times 10 + 1 + 1 = 65\).

docs.title: 9.6 Function calls and the stack
docs.text:
jal jumps to a routine and records the return address, the address of the instruction after the jal, in ra; ret jumps back through ra. The stack is a region of memory used to save values during calls. It grows downwards, and sp always points at its top. To push, subtract from sp and then store; to pop, load and then add back. A function must leave sp exactly where it found it before it returns.

main:
    addi a0, zero, 5      # argument: a0 = 5
    jal  ra, double       # call; ra = return address
    jal  zero, end        # (afterwards a0 holds 10)

double:                   # int double(int x) { return x + x; }
    addi sp, sp, -4       # make room on the stack
    sw   ra, 0(sp)        # save the return address
    add  a0, a0, a0       # a0 = x + x
    lw   ra, 0(sp)        # get it back
    addi sp, sp, 4        # give the room back
    ret                   # jump back through ra
end:
    nop

Example 9.4: following ra and sp through the call

The instructions are at addresses 0 (addi a0), 4 (jal ra), 8 (jal zero), and double starts at 12. Each row shows the registers after the instruction.

Step Instruction a0 ra sp Memory 1 addi a0, zero, 5 5 0 1024 2 jal ra, double 5 8 1024 3 addi sp, sp, -4 5 8 1020 4 sw ra, 0(sp) 5 8 1020 M[1020] = 8 5 add a0, a0, a0 10 8 1020 M[1020] = 8 6 lw ra, 0(sp) 10 8 1020 M[1020] = 8 7 addi sp, sp, 4 10 8 1024 M[1020] = 8 8 ret 10 8 1024 the PC jumps to 8

ra = 8 because the jal is at address 4, and the return address is the instruction after it. sp ends exactly where it started, and a0 holds the result, 10.

docs.title: Why save ra at all?
docs.text: This double calls no one, so it could skip the stack entirely: such a function is called a leaf. But suppose double itself called another function with jal ra, .... That would overwrite ra, and the way back to main would be lost. Saving ra on the stack before the call and restoring it before ret makes calls inside calls safe, however deep they go. Think of breadcrumbs: each call drops a crumb (the return address) on a pile, and each return picks up the top one. The pile is the stack.

docs.title: Recursion
docs.text:
A recursive function makes the stack visible. We compute \(\text{sumto}(n) = n + \text{sumto}(n-1)\) with \(\text{sumto}(0) = 0\). Each call that does not stop pushes two words, the return address and \(n\) (8 bytes), calls itself with \(n - 1\), then pops them and adds.

main:
    addi a0, zero, 10     # n = 10
    jal  ra, sumto
    jal  zero, end        # afterwards a0 = 55

sumto:                    # a0 = n on entry, result in a0
    beq  a0, zero, base   # n == 0: return 0 (a0 is already 0)
    addi sp, sp, -8       # push a frame of two words
    sw   ra, 4(sp)        # save the return address
    sw   a0, 0(sp)        # save n
    addi a0, a0, -1       # argument n - 1
    jal  ra, sumto        # recursive call: a0 = sumto(n - 1)
    lw   t0, 0(sp)        # restore n
    lw   ra, 4(sp)        # restore the return address
    addi sp, sp, 8        # pop the frame
    add  a0, a0, t0       # result = sumto(n - 1) + n
    ret
base:
    ret
end:
    nop

The base case returns at once, without touching the stack. Every other call pushes one 8-byte frame, and there are ten of them in the deepest chain (\(n = 10\) down to \(n = 1\)), so the deepest value of sp is \(1024 - 10 \times 8 = 944\) (Figure 9.2). Each frame holds the saved \(n\) and the return address: the frame of \(n = 10\) holds the return address 8 (back into main), and every other frame holds 36, the address of the lw after the recursive jal. After the last return, sp is back at 1024 and a0 = 55.
