Figure 9.2. The stack pointer during sumto(10): it falls by 8 on each of ten nested calls, reaches 944, and then rises back to 1024 as the calls return.

docs.title: 9.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Predict, then step. Only a prediction that can be wrong proves understanding. A trace table keeps the score; always read its last row.
  • The logic instructions work bit by bit, and a left shift by \(n\) multiplies by \(2^n\).
  • Memory is byte-addressed: words are 4 bytes, so successive word addresses go up in 4s. A store copies a value; changing the register afterwards does not change memory.
  • A loop tested at the bottom saves a jump on every pass: 33 instructions instead of 45 for the same sum. An off-by-one error appears in the last row of the trace.
  • jal puts the return address in ra; the stack saves values across nested calls; sp must come back to where it began.
  • Instruction counts depend on how a loop is written, so state the layout when you quote a count.

docs.title: 9.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 9.1 (the larger of two numbers). With t0 = 23 and t1 = 41, which add runs and how many instructions run in total?

    addi t0, zero, 23
    addi t1, zero, 41
    blt  t0, t1, second
    add  a0, zero, t0       # first is the larger
    jal  zero, done
second:
    add  a0, zero, t1       # second is the larger
done:
    nop

Then swap the values; then change one instruction so that a0 receives the smaller value.

Answer

\(23 < 41\), so blt jumps to second, and a0 = 41. The instructions executed are addi, addi, blt, add (at second) and nop: 5 in all. With t0 = 41 and t1 = 23, blt falls through, add a0, zero, t0 runs, then jal jumps over second, then nop: a0 = 41 again, in 6 instructions. To obtain the smaller value, change blt to bge: now second is entered when \(t0 \ge t1\), and the fall-through path is the one for \(t0 < t1\), so a0 receives the smaller.

Exercise 9.2 (read machine code back). A memory dump shows the word 0x00A00513. What instruction is it?

Answer

Write it as 32 bits: 000000001010 00000 000 01010 0010011. The opcode 0010011 is I-type arithmetic, with funct3 = 000, which is addi; rs1 = x0 = zero, rd = x10 = a0, and the immediate is 10. The instruction is addi a0, zero, 10, also written li a0, 10.

Exercise 9.3. A program stores three words with sw, starting at address 200. At which addresses do the second and third words start? And after any correct function call returns, what must sp be?

Answer

Words are 4 bytes apart in a byte-addressed memory, so the second word starts at 204 and the third at 208. After a correct call returns, sp must be exactly the value it had before the call: every push is matched by a pop, so the caller finds the stack as it left it.

Exercise 9.4 (four small programs). Write each in RV32I assembly, ending with nop, predict the result and the number of instructions executed, then check by tracing: (a) the sum \(1 + \dots + 100\) in a0, testing at the bottom of the loop; (b) \(7 \times 6\) by repeated addition (RV32I has no multiply instruction); (c) the number of 1 bits in 0xB5, using andi and srli; (d) the largest of 17, 42 and 30, using bge.

Answer

(a) Change the limit register of Section 9.4 to 101: a0 = 5050, and \(3 + 100 \times 3 = 303\) instructions with the bottom test.

(b) Add 7 to the accumulator six times:

    addi a0, zero, 0
    addi t0, zero, 7
    addi t1, zero, 6      # counter
loop:
    beq  t1, zero, done
    add  a0, a0, t0
    addi t1, t1, -1
    jal  zero, loop
done:
    nop

The results are a0 = 42; the count is \(3 + 6 \times 4 + 1 + 1 = 29\) instructions.

(c) \(\text{0xB5} = 1011\,0101\), which has five 1 bits:

    addi t0, zero, 0xB5
    addi a0, zero, 0
loop:
    beq  t0, zero, done
    andi t1, t0, 1        # lowest bit
    add  a0, a0, t1       # add it to the count
    srli t0, t0, 1        # shift the next bit down
    jal  zero, loop
done:
    nop

The result is a0 = 5. The loop runs eight times (while t0 takes the values 181, 90, 45, 22, 11, 5, 2, 1), so there are \(2 + 8 \times 5 + 1 + 1 = 44\) instructions.

(d) Keep the largest so far in a0:

    addi t0, zero, 17
    addi t1, zero, 42
    addi t2, zero, 30
    add  a0, zero, t0
    bge  a0, t1, s1       # keep a0 if it is already >= t1
    add  a0, zero, t1
s1:
    bge  a0, t2, s2
    add  a0, zero, t2
s2:
    nop

The result is a0 = 42; the first bge falls through (17 < 42) and the second jumps (42 ≥ 30), so 8 instructions run. In every case the counts depend on how the loops are written.

Exercise 9.5 (a recursive function and the stack). Write \(\text{sumto}(n) = n + \text{sumto}(n-1)\), \(\text{sumto}(0) = 0\), as a real recursive function, call it from main with \(n = 10\), and record the deepest value of sp. What must the program print for a0 and the final sp?

Answer

The program is the one in Section 9.6. Each of the ten nested calls pushes a frame of 8 bytes (the return address and \(n\)), so the deepest sp is \(1024 - 80 = 944\). The result is a0 = 55, and sp returns to 1024. A trace of the stack at the deepest point (from the top of the stack downwards) holds, for the frame of \(n = 10\), the return address 8 at 1020 and \(n = 10\) at 1016; for \(n = 9\), the return address 36 at 1012 and 9 at 1008; and so on down to \(n = 1\), with 36 at 948 and 1 at 944.

Exercise 9.6. In Example 9.4, why does the program survive if double is changed to call another function helper (so that jal ra, helper appears inside it), provided it saves ra first? What would happen if it did not?

Answer

The call to helper overwrites ra with the address of the instruction after that second jal. Because double saved the original ra (the way back to main) on the stack beforehand, it can reload it with lw ra, 0(sp) just before ret, and the return goes to the right place. Without the save, ret would jump to the instruction inside double that follows the call to helper, not to main; the way back to the caller would be lost and the program would misbehave.

docs.title: Chapter 8: RISC-V: The Instruction Set
docs.text: An instruction set is the contract between the software you write and the hardware that runs it. This chapter introduces RISC-V, an open and modular instruction set that has become the standard vehicle for teaching computer architecture and is used in real products from sensors to servers. It explains what an instruction set architecture is and what "open" means, how RISC-V is built from a small base and optional extensions, the RISC design philosophy, the 32 registers and their conventional roles, and the six instruction formats, which you will learn to encode and decode by hand. We work with RV32I, the 32-bit base integer instruction set: the smallest complete core and ideal for learning.

docs.title: 8.1 What an instruction set is
docs.text:
An instruction set architecture (ISA) is the list of instructions that a processor understands, the registers it offers, how memory is addressed, and exactly how each instruction is encoded as bits. It is a specification, not a chip. Many different chips, from a tiny microcontroller to a 64-core server part, can implement the same ISA and run the very same program files. An ISA is like the standard for a power socket: any appliance built to the standard works in any socket built to it, whoever made either one.

RISC-V (pronounced "risk five") is such a specification, with one radical difference: it is open and free. Anyone may design, manufacture and sell a RISC-V processor without paying a licence fee or asking permission. Compare the position of other families.

ISA Who controls it To build a chip that runs it x86 Intel and AMD in effect, you cannot Arm Arm Ltd. buy a licence and pay royalties RISC-V RISC-V International, a non-profit just do it: no fee, no permission

RISC-V was born at the University of California, Berkeley, in 2010, as a clean-slate design for teaching and research.

What open means

"Open" here means that the specification is freely usable, like an open standard such as TCP/IP or USB. It does not mean that every implementation is open-source silicon: companies may still sell closed chips that implement the ISA. What is guaranteed is that the encoding and the meaning of the instructions belong to everyone.

Why does an open ISA matter?

  • No lock-in. A start-up, a university or a national laboratory can build a processor without negotiating a licence.
  • Modularity. You implement only what you need, so a tiny sensor chip and a server processor share one base.
  • Stability for learning. The base ISA is small, frozen and completely documented, so what you learn stays true.
  • A shared ecosystem. Compilers (GCC, LLVM), operating systems (Linux) and tools all target one open target, so every chip gets software for free.

docs.title: 8.2 A small base and optional extensions
docs.text:
RISC-V is built like a construction set: one mandatory brick, and standard bricks that you add only if you need them. Each standard extension has a single-letter name.

Letter Name What it adds I base integer integer registers, load and store, arithmetic, branches, jumps: enough to run any program M multiply and divide mul, div, rem and relatives A atomics indivisible read-modify-write operations for several cores sharing memory F, D floating point 32-bit and 64-bit IEEE-754 numbers and their own registers C compressed 16-bit versions of common instructions, to make programs smaller

The combination I, M, A, F and D is so common for general-purpose computing that it has the shorthand G. The width of the registers is chosen separately and written first: RV32 (32-bit), RV64 (64-bit) and even RV128. So RV32IMC is a 32-bit core with the base integer set, multiply and divide, and compressed instructions: a typical microcontroller. RV64GC is a 64-bit core with integer, multiply, atomics, single- and double-precision floating point, and compressed instructions: the sweet spot for running Linux. This chapter and the next two work with RV32I.

docs.title: 8.3 The RISC philosophy
docs.text:
The "RISC" in RISC-V stands for Reduced Instruction Set Computer. This design school keeps each instruction simple, regular and fast, and lets the compiler build complicated things from simple pieces. Its opposite, CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer, for example x86), offers many powerful instructions of varying length, so that one instruction may do a lot.

RISC-V's flavour of RISC rests on three rules.

  1. Load-store architecture. Only loads and stores touch memory. Arithmetic works on registers only.
  2. Fixed-length instructions. Every base instruction is exactly 32 bits (4 bytes) long. Fetching and decoding are then trivial, and pipelines are regular. (The C extension adds optional 16-bit forms.)
  3. Few, regular formats. There are only six instruction layouts, with the register fields in the same bit positions in all of them, so the hardware can start reading registers before it has finished decoding.

To add a number from memory to a register, x86 needs one instruction of variable length, and RISC-V needs two simple ones:

; x86 (CISC): one instruction, reads memory and adds
add eax, [ebx]

# RISC-V (RISC): two simple instructions
lw  t0, 0(a1)       # load from memory
add a0, a0, t0      # then add
RISC-V x86 Instruction length fixed, 4 bytes (base) variable, 1 to 15 bytes Arithmetic on memory no: load first yes Number of formats 6 many, irregular Decoding simple complex; often split into simpler internal steps Design aim simple hardware, clever compiler compact code, powerful instructions

Simplicity is a strategy, not a limitation. Uniform, cheap instructions let the hardware run more of them per second and pipeline them cleanly. The complexity moves into the compiler, which runs once, and out of the silicon, which runs forever.

docs.title: 8.4 Registers and the program counter
docs.text:
RV32I has 32 general-purpose registers, x0 to x31, each 32 bits wide. Nearly every instruction reads or writes them. One of them is special: x0 is wired to zero. Reading it always gives 0, and writing it does nothing. This gives a free constant and a place to throw results away, and it lets several useful instructions (mv, nop) be built from others at no cost in hardware.

The program counter (PC) holds the address of the current instruction. It is not one of the 32 registers, and you cannot name it as an operand. It moves on by 4 after each instruction, unless a branch or jump changes it.

Software follows a calling convention, the ABI (application binary interface), that gives each register a role, so that functions written by different people work together. It is a convention, not hardware. The ABI names are what you write in real assembly.

Registers ABI names Role Preserved across a call? x0 zero the constant 0 (writes ignored) not applicable x1 ra return address (set by jal) no (caller-saved) x2 sp stack pointer yes (callee-saved) x3, x4 gp, tp global and thread pointers fixed x5–x7, x28–x31 t0–t6 temporaries (scratch) no (caller-saved) x8–x9, x18–x27 s0–s11 saved registers (s0 is also the frame pointer) yes (callee-saved) x10–x17 a0–a7 function arguments; a0 and a1 also carry return values no (caller-saved)

The split between caller-saved and callee-saved is the heart of the convention. The temporaries and argument registers (t0–t6, a0–a7, ra) may be overwritten by a function that you call; if you need their values afterwards, save them yourself before the call. The saved registers (s0–s11) and sp are promised to look the same when the function returns, so a function that uses one must save and restore it. An analogy: you lend your desk for an hour. The temporaries are scrap paper, which the borrower may scribble on; the saved registers are your files, which whoever uses them must put back exactly as they were.

docs.title: 8.5 The six instruction formats
docs.text:
Every RV32I instruction is 32 bits, laid out in one of six patterns, named R, I, S, B, U and J (Figure 8.1). Look down the columns: the opcode is always the low 7 bits, and rd, rs1, rs2 and funct3 never move. The decoder can start reading registers before it even knows which format it has.

Figure 8.1. The six RV32I instruction formats, aligned by bit position. The sign bit of every immediate is bit 31.

docs.title: R-type: register with register
docs.text: Two source registers, one destination, no immediate. The fields funct7 and funct3 choose the operation: changing funct7 from 0000000 to 0100000 turns add into sub.

docs.title: I-type: a register and a constant
docs.text: One source register and a 12-bit immediate, which is sign-extended: its top bit is copied leftwards to fill 32 bits, so the immediate can be negative (\(-2048\) to \(2047\), that is \(-2^{11}\) to \(2^{11}-1\)). It is used by addi and the other immediate arithmetic, by loads (lw) and by jalr.

docs.title: S-type: stores
docs.text: A store needs two source registers (the address base and the data) but writes no register, so there is no rd. The 12-bit immediate is split into two pieces, imm[11:5] and imm[4:0], to keep rs1 and rs2 in their usual places.

docs.title: B-type: conditional branches
docs.text: If the comparison holds, the PC moves by the offset; otherwise it moves on by 4. The offset counts in 2-byte steps, so bit 0 is not stored, and the stored bits are shuffled (see below). The field funct3 picks the test: 000 is beq, 001 is bne, 100 is blt and 101 is bge.

docs.title: U-type and J-type
docs.text: U-type puts a 20-bit constant in the upper 20 bits of a register: lui a0, 0x10 gives 0x00010000. auipc adds such a constant to the PC. J-type is jal: a jump by a 20-bit offset that also writes the return address, PC + 4, into rd. Using jal zero, loop throws the return address away in x0, which is an unconditional jump.

docs.title: Why are the immediate bits scrambled?
docs.text:
The odd orderings of the immediates in S, B, U and J formats are not untidiness. The immediate's sign bit is always bit 31, so sign extension can start before the format is even known; and where formats share an immediate bit, it is placed on the same wire, so that B reuses S's layout and J reuses U's. The circuit that rebuilds an immediate then needs far fewer multiplexers. What looks untidy to a human is tidy for the hardware, which reads every instruction billions of times a second. Figure 8.2 shows how the branch offset is assembled.

Figure 8.2. How the B-type offset is reassembled from the instruction word. Bit 31 supplies the sign of the offset.

docs.title: 8.6 The core instruction set
docs.text:
The working vocabulary of RV32I is short.

Group Instructions Meaning Arithmetic add, sub, addi rd = rs1 ± rs2 (or + a constant) Logic and, or, xor, andi, ori, xori bit by bit Shifts sll, srl, sra, slli, srli, srai left; right logical (0s in); right arithmetic (sign copied) Compare slt, sltu, slti, sltiu rd = 1 if rs1 < rs2 (signed or unsigned), else 0 Memory lw, lh, lb, lbu, lhu; sw, sh, sb load or store a word, half-word or byte Branch beq, bne, blt, bge, bltu, bgeu compare, and maybe jump Jump jal, jalr jump and remember PC + 4 Upper lui, auipc rd = constant << 12 (auipc adds the PC)

Assemblers also accept friendly shorthands, called pseudo-instructions, which they turn into one or more real instructions.

You write It becomes Why it works li a0, 42 addi a0, zero, 42 0 + 42 mv a0, t0 addi a0, t0, 0 t0 + 0 nop addi zero, zero, 0 a write to x0 changes nothing j label jal zero, label jump, and throw the return address away ret jalr zero, 0(ra) jump to the address in ra

Pseudo-instructions cost no hardware, and two of them exist only because x0 is always zero.

docs.title: 8.7 Encoding and decoding by hand
docs.text:
To encode an instruction, find its format, write each field in binary, and join the fields from bit 31 down to bit 0. To decode, write the 8 hexadecimal digits as 32 bits, read the low 7 bits (the opcode) to find the format, and cut the rest along that format's fields.

Example 8.1: encoding add x7, x5, x6

add is R-type with opcode 0110011, funct3 = 000 and funct7 = 0000000. The registers are rd = x7, rs1 = x5 and rs2 = x6.

Field funct7 rs2 rs1 funct3 rd opcode Value 0000000 00110 00101 000 00111 0110011

Joined: 0000000 00110 00101 000 00111 0110011 = 0000 0000 0110 0010 1000 0011 1011 0011 = 0x006283B3. Changing funct7 to 0100000 gives sub x7, x5, x6, which is 0x406283B3.

Example 8.2: immediates, including a negative one

addi a0, zero, 10 is I-type (opcode 0010011, funct3 = 000) with imm = 10 = 000000001010, rs1 = x0, rd = x10:

000000001010 00000 000 01010 0010011 = 0x00A00513.

For addi t2, t2, -1 the immediate is \(-1\), which in twelve bits is 111111111111; t2 is x7, so rs1 = rd = 00111:

111111111111 00111 000 00111 0010011 = 0xFFF38393.

The sign-extension of the immediate turns that into \(-1\) in 32 bits.

Example 8.3: loads and stores

lw a0, 8(sp) is I-type (opcode 0000011, funct3 = 010), with imm = 8, rs1 = sp = x2 and rd = a0 = x10:

000000001000 00010 010 01010 0000011 = 0x00812503.

sw a0, 0(sp) is S-type (opcode 0100011, funct3 = 010), with rs2 = a0 = x10, rs1 = sp = x2 and imm = 0. The immediate is split: imm[11:5] = 0000000 and imm[4:0] = 00000:

0000000 01010 00010 010 00000 0100011 = 0x00A12023.

With a non-zero offset, sw a0, 8(sp) has imm = 8 = 0000000_01000, so imm[11:5] = 0000000 and imm[4:0] = 01000 and the code is 0x00A12423: the low five bits of the offset sit in the rd position of the word.

Example 8.4: branches

beq t0, t1, 8 is B-type (opcode 1100011, funct3 = 000), with rs1 = t0 = x5 and rs2 = t1 = x6. The offset is \(8 = 0\,0000\,0000\,1000\) as a 13-bit number, so imm[12] = 0, imm[11] = 0, imm[10:5] = 000000 and imm[4:1] = 0100. Joined as imm[12] imm[10:5], rs2, rs1, funct3, imm[4:1] imm[11], opcode:

0 000000 00110 00101 000 0100 0 1100011 = 0x00628463.

Now the backward branch bne t0, t1, -8 (funct3 = 001). The offset \(-8\) in 13 bits is 1 1111 1111 1000, so imm[12] = 1, imm[11] = 1, imm[10:5] = 111111 and imm[4:1] = 1100:

1 111111 00110 00101 001 1100 1 1100011 = 0xFE629CE3.

The negative offset fills the high immediate bits with 1s: that is the sign bit, extended.

Example 8.5: decoding three words

The opcode (low 7 bits) tells the format.

  • 0x406283B3 = 0100000 00110 00101 000 00111 0110011. The opcode 0110011 is R-type; funct7 = 0100000 with funct3 = 000 means sub; rs2 = 6, rs1 = 5, rd = 7. This is sub x7, x5, x6.
  • 0xFFF38393 = 111111111111 00111 000 00111 0010011. The opcode 0010011 is I-type arithmetic with funct3 = 000, which is addi; imm = −1, rs1 = rd = x7. This is addi t2, t2, -1.
  • 0x00010537 = 00000000000000010000 01010 0110111. The opcode 0110111 is lui; rd = 10, imm = 0x00010. This is lui a0, 0x10.

docs.title: Building a 32-bit constant
docs.text:
A 32-bit constant needs a lui for the upper 20 bits and an addi for the lower 12. Because addi sign-extends its 12-bit immediate, there is one catch: when bit 11 of the constant is 1, the addi will subtract, and the lui must be one larger to compensate. The assembler's li does this automatically.

Example 8.6: li t0, 0x12345678 and li t0, 0x12345FFF

For 0x12345678, the low 12 bits are 0x678, whose top bit is 0, so lui t0, 0x12345 followed by addi t0, t0, 0x678 gives 0x12345000 + 0x678 = 0x12345678.

For 0x12345FFF, the low 12 bits 0xFFF are \(-1\) as a signed immediate. Using lui t0, 0x12345 and addi t0, t0, -1 would give 0x12345000 - 1 = 0x12344FFF, which is wrong. The correct pair is lui t0, 0x12346 (giving 0x12346000) and addi t0, t0, -1, which gives 0x12346000 - 1 = 0x12345FFF.

docs.title: 8.8 Summary
docs.text:
• An ISA is the contract between software and hardware. RISC-V's is open: anyone may implement it without a licence.
  • RISC-V has a small base (RV32I) plus optional one-letter extensions; G is IMAFD; the register width comes first (RV32, RV64).
  • The RISC creed: load-store, fixed 32-bit instructions, six formats with register fields that never move. The complexity is left to the compiler.
  • RV32I has 32 registers of 32 bits, with x0 always zero; the PC is separate. The ABI names the registers and says who saves what: temporaries and arguments are caller-saved, s registers and sp callee-saved.
  • The formats are R, I, S, B, U and J. Immediates are sign-extended, and the sign is always bit 31; the scrambled bits of S, B, U and J keep the immediate wiring small.
  • Pseudo-instructions such as li, mv, nop, j and ret are real instructions in disguise, and some exist only because x0 is zero.
  • To encode, find the format and join the fields; to decode, read the opcode first. A 32-bit constant is built with lui and addi, adjusting lui when bit 11 of the constant is set.

docs.title: 8.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 8.1. A datasheet says RV32IMC, and another says RV64GC. What does each chip support?

Answer

RV32IMC: 32-bit registers, the base integer set, multiply and divide, and compressed 16-bit instructions: a typical microcontroller. RV64GC: 64-bit registers, I + M + A + F + D (the G group: integer, multiply and divide, atomics, single- and double-precision floating point) and compressed instructions: the kind of core that boots Linux.

Exercise 8.2 (encode by hand). Write the fields in binary, then in hexadecimal: (a) add x7, x5, x6; (b) addi a0, zero, 10; (c) lw a0, 8(sp); (d) sw a0, 0(sp); (e) beq t0, t1, 8.

Answer

(a) 0000000 00110 00101 000 00111 0110011 = 0x006283B3. (b) 000000001010 00000 000 01010 0010011 = 0x00A00513. (c) 000000001000 00010 010 01010 0000011 = 0x00812503. (d) 0000000 01010 00010 010 00000 0100011 = 0x00A12023. (e) 0 000000 00110 00101 000 0100 0 1100011 = 0x00628463.

Exercise 8.3 (decode by hand). Find the format from the opcode first, then decode: 0x406283B3, 0xFFF38393, 0x00010537.

Answer

0x406283B3 is sub x7, x5, x6 (R-type, funct7 = 0100000). 0xFFF38393 is addi t2, t2, -1 (I-type, immediate 0xFFF \(= -1\)). 0x00010537 is lui a0, 0x10 (U-type, upper immediate 0x00010, destination x10). Section 8.7 gives the fields.

Exercise 8.4. Encode sw t1, 4(t0), with t1 = x6 and t0 = x5.

Answer

S-type, opcode 0100011, funct3 = 010, rs2 = x6 = 00110, rs1 = x5 = 00101, imm = 4 = 0000000_00100, so imm[11:5] = 0000000 and imm[4:0] = 00100:

0000000 00110 00101 010 00100 0100011 = 0000 0000 0110 0010 1010 0010 0010 0011 = 0x0062A223.

Exercise 8.5. Why can mv and nop exist without any extra hardware?

Answer

Because they are not real instructions. mv rd, rs is addi rd, rs, 0, which adds zero to rs and writes the result to rd. nop is addi zero, zero, 0, which adds zero to x0 and writes the result back to x0, a write that is ignored. Both work only because addi exists and because x0 is always zero.

Exercise 8.6. A load word instruction lw t0, 100(a1) is followed by add a0, a0, t0. Why does the RISC-V version of "add a word from memory to a register" take two instructions, while x86 can do it in one? Give one advantage of the RISC-V approach.

Answer

RISC-V is a load-store architecture: arithmetic instructions work only on registers, and only lw/sw touch memory, so the memory read and the add are separate instructions. An x86 instruction can name a memory operand directly, so one instruction (of variable length) does both. The advantage of the RISC-V approach is regularity: every instruction is 4 bytes and has few formats, so it is easy to fetch and decode, and only one pipeline stage ever accesses data memory. Complexity moves into the compiler.

Exercise 8.7. What 32-bit pair of instructions loads the constant 0xDEADBEEF into a0? (Hint: the low 12 bits are 0xEEF, whose top bit is 1.)

Answer

The low 12 bits 0xEEF have bit 11 set, so as a signed immediate they equal \(0xEEF - 0x1000 = -273\). addi will therefore subtract, and the upper part must be one larger: the upper 20 bits 0xDEADB plus 1 is 0xDEADC. The pair is lui a0, 0xDEADC followed by addi a0, a0, -273 (the same as addi a0, a0, 0xEEF written as a 12-bit immediate). Check: \(0xDEADC000 - 273 = 0xDEADC000 - 0x111 = 0xDEADBEEF\).

docs.title: Chapter 5: Verilog: Building, Testing and Debugging Designs
docs.text: The previous two chapters taught the constructs. This chapter uses them. It first adds the tools for handling many bits at once (vectors, concatenation, parameters and generate), then builds a useful circuit bottom-up, from a full adder through a ripple-carry adder to a small ALU, proves each piece with a testbench, and finishes with the bugs that nearly every beginner writes and how never to write them. Hardware that you cannot test is hardware that you cannot trust, so the testbench is treated as part of the design.

docs.title: 5.1 Vectors and concatenation
docs.text:
A multi-bit signal is a vector, declared with a range [msb:lsb]. The convention [N-1:0] puts bit 0, the least significant bit, on the right, as in the registers of Chapter 1.

wire [7:0] data;                  // 8 bits; data[7] is the most significant
wire [3:0] nibble;
wire       msb;
assign nibble = data[3:0];        // a part-select: the low four bits
assign msb    = data[7];          // a bit-select: one bit

Braces { , } build wider vectors by concatenation: the bits are placed side by side, the first item on the left. {n{x}} repeats x \(n\) times. No logic is built; it is only wiring.

Write Meaning Example result {byte1, byte0} join: byte1 becomes the top half 8'hAB, 8'hCD give 16'hABCD {data[6:0], data[7]} rotate left by one 1001_0110 becomes 0010_1101 {4'b0000, nibble} zero-extend 4 bits to 8 1011 becomes 0000_1011 {{4{n[3]}}, n} sign-extend: copy the sign bit 1011 (−5) becomes 1111_1011 (−5)

docs.title: 5.2 Parameters and generate
docs.text:
A parameter is a constant chosen when a module is used, so that one description serves any width. It is overridden at the instance with #( ).

module adder #(parameter WIDTH = 8) (
    input  wire [WIDTH-1:0] a, b,
    output wire [WIDTH:0]   sum       // one extra bit holds the carry
);
    assign sum = a + b;
endmodule

// a 16-bit copy:
// adder #(.WIDTH(16)) u_add (.a(x), .b(y), .sum(s));

The generate construct stamps out many copies of an instance while the design is being built (elaboration), which is ideal for arrays of identical blocks. The loop variable is a genvar, and each iteration is given a name.

genvar i;
generate
    for (i = 0; i < 8; i = i + 1) begin : slice
        full_adder fa (.a(a[i]), .b(b[i]), .cin(c[i]), .sum(s[i]), .cout(c[i+1]));
    end
endgenerate

This builds eight full adders in a chain, the carry-out of one feeding the carry-in of the next. It is not a loop that runs when the circuit works: the circuit contains eight adders.

docs.title: 5.3 A worked build: full adder, ripple adder, ALU
docs.text: Small pieces, combined bottom-up, make something useful. We build an adder and then an ALU, and test each.

docs.title: Step 1: a full adder
docs.text:
A full adder adds three bits (two operands and a carry in) and produces a sum bit and a carry out. The sum is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1; the carry out is 1 when at least two are, the majority function of Exercise 3.3.

module full_adder (
    input  wire a, b, cin,
    output wire sum, cout
);
    assign sum  = a ^ b ^ cin;
    assign cout = (a & b) | (a & cin) | (b & cin);
endmodule

docs.title: Step 2: a 4-bit ripple-carry adder
docs.text:
Chain four full adders (Figure 5.1); each carry out feeds the next carry in.

module ripple_adder4 (
    input  wire [3:0] a, b,
    input  wire       cin,
    output wire [3:0] sum,
    output wire       cout
);
    wire [3:1] c;      // c[k] is the carry into bit k
    full_adder fa0 (.a(a[0]), .b(b[0]), .cin(cin),  .sum(sum[0]), .cout(c[1]));
    full_adder fa1 (.a(a[1]), .b(b[1]), .cin(c[1]), .sum(sum[1]), .cout(c[2]));
    full_adder fa2 (.a(a[2]), .b(b[2]), .cin(c[2]), .sum(sum[2]), .cout(c[3]));
    full_adder fa3 (.a(a[3]), .b(b[3]), .cin(c[3]), .sum(sum[3]), .cout(cout));
endmodule
Figure 5.1. A 4-bit ripple-carry adder: four full adders, the carry passing from bit 0 towards bit 3.

Each stage must wait for the carry from the stage to its right. That waiting, the carry rippling along, is why a long adder is slow, and why faster adder designs exist.

Example 5.1: 11 + 6 on the ripple adder

Let a = 1011 (11), b = 0110 (6) and cin = 0. Working from bit 0:

Bit a b carry in sum carry out 0 1 0 0 1 0 1 1 1 0 0 1 2 0 1 1 0 1 3 1 0 1 0 1

Reading the sum bits from bit 3 down to bit 0 gives sum = 0001 with cout = 1: the five-bit result 1_0001 is 17, as it should be.

docs.title: Step 3: a small ALU
docs.text:
A 4-bit ALU chooses between add, subtract, AND and OR with a 2-bit operation code, and flags a zero result. Subtraction reuses the adder by the two's complement identity of Chapter 1, \(a - b = a + \overline{b} + 1\).

module alu4 (
    input  wire [3:0] a, b,
    input  wire [1:0] op,        // 00 add  01 sub  10 and  11 or
    output reg  [3:0] result,
    output reg        carry,     // carry out (for sub: 1 means no borrow)
    output wire       zero       // 1 when result == 0
);
    reg [4:0] tmp;               // 5 bits: room for the carry
    always @(*) begin
        carry  = 1'b0;
        result = 4'b0000;
        tmp    = 5'b00000;
        case (op)
            2'b00: begin tmp = {1'b0, a} + {1'b0, b};
                         result = tmp[3:0]; carry = tmp[4]; end
            2'b01: begin tmp = {1'b0, a} + {1'b0, ~b} + 5'd1;
                         result = tmp[3:0]; carry = tmp[4]; end
            2'b10: result = a & b;
            2'b11: result = a | b;
        endcase
    end
    assign zero = (result == 4'b0000);
endmodule

A trap in the subtract line

The tempting line tmp = a + (~b) + 5'd1; looks right and is wrong. Verilog first widens every operand to the size of the whole expression, here five bits because tmp has five bits, and only then inverts. For b = 0100, ~b becomes 1_1011, not 1011. The four-bit difference still comes out right, but carry is inverted: it reads 0 when no borrow occurred and 1 when one did. Writing {1'b0, ~b} says exactly what is meant, because inside braces each item keeps its own width, so ~b is inverted at four bits and only then given a leading 0. The lesson is general: in Verilog the width of an expression is decided by its context, so when widths differ, write the extension out yourself.

The numbers to check by hand are collected in the next section, together with the testbench that produces them.

docs.title: 5.4 Testbenches: simulating your design
docs.text:
A testbench is a Verilog module with no ports. It is never built into hardware. Inside it, you place your design, the device under test (DUT), wire its pins, change the inputs over time and watch the outputs. Because it is never synthesised, it may use delays and printing.

Construct What it does initial runs once, starting at time 0: the place for stimulus #10 wait 10 time units before the next statement $display(...) print once, like printf $monitor(...) print again automatically whenever a listed signal changes $dumpfile, $dumpvars record every signal to a waveform file, to view in GTKWave $finish end the simulation

A first testbench for the ALU drives five operations and prints the results:

`timescale 1ns/1ps
module alu4_tb;
    reg  [3:0] a, b;                       // drive these
    reg  [1:0] op;
    wire [3:0] result;                     // watch these
    wire       carry, zero;

    alu4 dut (.a(a), .b(b), .op(op),
              .result(result), .carry(carry), .zero(zero));

    initial $monitor("op=%b a=%d b=%d -> result=%d carry=%b zero=%b",
                     op, a, b, result, carry, zero);

    initial begin
        a = 3; b = 5; op = 2'b00; #10;     // 3 + 5
        a = 9; b = 4; op = 2'b01; #10;     // 9 - 4
        a = 6; b = 3; op = 2'b10; #10;     // 0110 & 0011
        a = 8; b = 8; op = 2'b01; #10;     // 8 - 8: zero
        $finish;
    end
endmodule

What the simulator prints is

op=00 a= 3 b= 5 -> result= 8 carry=0 zero=0
op=01 a= 9 b= 4 -> result= 5 carry=1 zero=0
op=10 a= 6 b= 3 -> result= 2 carry=0 zero=0
op=01 a= 8 b= 8 -> result= 0 carry=1 zero=1

Check each line by hand, because that is the habit that finds bugs. For 9 - 4, the subtract path computes \(01001 + 01011 + 1 = 10101\), so result = 0101 (5) and carry = tmp[4] = 1 (no borrow). For 8 - 8, it computes \(01000 + 00111 + 1 = 10000\), so result = 0000, carry = 1 and zero = 1. The AND line is \(0110 \wedge 0011 = 0010 = 2\).

To record waveforms, add

initial begin
    $dumpfile("alu4.vcd");
    $dumpvars(0, alu4_tb);
end

and open alu4.vcd in GTKWave. A waveform shows when things happen, which a printed list cannot.

docs.title: Self-checking testbenches
docs.text: A testbench that only prints needs a person to read the output, and people miss errors, especially among hundreds of cases. A good testbench judges itself: it computes the expected answer, compares, counts the failures and prints PASS or FAIL. Exercise 5.5 builds one that tries all 1 536 combinations of an extended ALU.

docs.title: 5.5 Pitfalls
docs.text: Three bugs are written by nearly every beginner, and a fourth catches the careful as well.

docs.title: The accidental latch
docs.text:
If a combinational always @(*) block does not assign an output on every path (a missing else, an uncovered case), the output must remember its old value, so synthesis builds a latch: memory in combinational logic. It is almost never what you wanted and a source of timing trouble.

// BAD: no else, so y holds its old value and a latch is inferred
always @(*) begin
    if (sel) y = a;
end

// GOOD: a default first, so every path gives y a value
always @(*) begin
    y = 1'b0;
    if (sel) y = a;
end

A full else, or a default in a case, works too. The cure is a habit: assign every output a default at the top of the block.

docs.title: The incomplete sensitivity list
docs.text:
In old-style blocks such as always @(a or b), forgetting a signal (here c) makes simulation and hardware disagree: the simulator ignores changes on c, but the synthesised gates do not.

always @(a or b)          // c is missing!
    y = a & b & c;

The fix is to always write @(*) and let the tool build the list.

docs.title: Blocking assignment in clocked logic
docs.text:
Using = inside always @(posedge clk) can create race conditions and mismatches between simulation and synthesis, especially when one register feeds another.

always @(posedge clk) begin
    b = a;      // b changes now...
    c = b;      // ...so c gets the new b
end

This builds one flip-flop stage where you may have meant two, and its behaviour can depend on the order in which other blocks happen to run. The fix is <= for every clocked assignment.

docs.title: Expression width
docs.text:
The trap in the subtract line (Section 5.3) is the same family of bug: widths decided by context. The tool will not warn you; the testbench will, if it checks the carry as well as the result.

Questions to ask of every block

Is this block combinational or clocked? If combinational, does every output get a value on every path, and is the sensitivity list @(*)? If clocked, are all assignments non-blocking, and does the reset (if any) cover every register? Are all widths in each expression equal?

docs.title: 5.6 Summary
docs.text:
• A vector is declared [N-1:0]; concatenation joins bits (no logic), {n{x}} repeats them, and the common forms rotate, zero-extend and sign-extend.
  • Parameters make a module serve any width; generate builds repeated structure at elaboration time.
  • Build bottom-up: a full adder, a ripple adder (slow because the carry ripples), an ALU, and test each piece.
  • In an expression, width comes from context. Write {1'b0, ~b} rather than relying on widening.
  • A testbench has no ports, uses initial, delays and $display or $monitor, and is never synthesised. A self-checking testbench compares with expected values itself and prints PASS or FAIL.
  • The big bugs: accidental latches (give every output a default), incomplete sensitivity lists (use @(*)), blocking assignments in clocked blocks (use <=), and expression-width mistakes.

docs.title: 5.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 5.1. Trace the 4-bit ripple adder for a = 0111, b = 0001, cin = 0 bit by bit. What does it show about the speed of a ripple adder?

Answer Bit a b carry in sum carry out 0 1 1 0 0 1 1 1 0 1 0 1 2 1 0 1 0 1 3 0 0 1 1 0

The result is sum = 1000 (8) with cout = 0: \(7 + 1 = 8\). The carry created at bit 0 had to travel through all the stages before bit 3 could settle, so the delay of the adder grows with its width. This is the worst case for a ripple adder.

Exercise 5.2. Use parameter and generate to write an \(N\)-bit ripple-carry adder from the full_adder module.

Answer 
module ripple_adder #(parameter N = 8) (
    input  wire [N-1:0] a, b,
    input  wire         cin,
    output wire [N-1:0] sum,
    output wire         cout
);
    wire [N:0] c;                 // carry chain: N + 1 wires
    assign c[0] = cin;
    genvar i;
    generate
        for (i = 0; i < N; i = i + 1) begin : stage
            full_adder fa (.a(a[i]), .b(b[i]), .cin(c[i]),
                           .sum(sum[i]), .cout(c[i+1]));
        end
    endgenerate
    assign cout = c[N];
endmodule

The instance is ripple_adder #(.N(16)) u (...) for 16 bits. For synthesis one would usually write the one-line behavioural alternative, assign {cout, sum} = a + b + cin;, and let the tool choose a good adder; the structural version shows how generate and hierarchy work.

Exercise 5.3. For alu4, work out the three outputs result, carry and zero for op = 01 (subtract) with (a) a = 7, b = 9; (b) a = 5, b = 5. Then give the output of the faulty line tmp = a + (~b) + 5'd1; for case (a), and say what is wrong with it.

Answer

(a) \(a - b = -2\). With the correct line, \(00111 + 00110 + 1 = 01110\), so result = 1110 (which is \(-2\) in 4-bit two's complement), carry = 0 (a borrow occurred), zero = 0. (b) \(00101 + 01010 + 1 = 10000\), so result = 0000, carry = 1, zero = 1. With the faulty line, in case (a) ~b is evaluated at five bits as 10110, so the sum is \(00111 + 10110 + 1 = 11110\) (five bits), and result = 1110 is still right but carry = tmp[4] = 1, the opposite of the correct 0. The carry flag is inverted by the context-widening of ~.

Exercise 5.4. What is the difference between $display and $monitor, and why can neither be used in a design that is to be synthesised?

Answer

$display prints once, at the moment the statement is executed; $monitor registers a message that is printed again automatically each time one of its listed signals changes. Both are simulation system tasks: they print to a screen or file, which no chip can do, so a synthesis tool ignores them or rejects them. The same is true of delays such as #10.

Exercise 5.5 (an ALU with a self-checking testbench). Extend the ALU to six operations: ADD, SUB, AND, OR, XOR and SLT (set the result to 1 if \(a < b\), unsigned, else 0), with outputs y, carry and zero. For SUB, compute {1'b0,a} + {1'b0,~b} + 5'd1, so that carry = 1 means "no borrow". Write a testbench that loops over all 256 pairs \((a, b)\) for each operation, compares with a reference computed in the testbench, counts errors and prints PASS or FAIL. How many cases are checked, and what do the hand-checked values below show?

Answer 
module alu6 (
    input  wire [3:0] a, b,
    input  wire [2:0] op,    // 000 add  001 sub  010 and  011 or  100 xor  101 slt
    output reg  [3:0] y,
    output reg        carry,
    output wire       zero
);
    reg [4:0] t;
    always @(*) begin
        t = 5'd0;  carry = 1'b0;
        case (op)
            3'b000: begin t = {1'b0, a} + {1'b0, b};
                          y = t[3:0]; carry = t[4]; end
            3'b001: begin t = {1'b0, a} + {1'b0, ~b} + 5'd1;
                          y = t[3:0]; carry = t[4]; end
            3'b010: y = a & b;
            3'b011: y = a | b;
            3'b100: y = a ^ b;
            3'b101: y = (a < b) ? 4'd1 : 4'd0;
            default: y = 4'd0;
        endcase
    end
    assign zero = (y == 4'd0);
endmodule

`timescale 1ns/1ps
module alu6_tb;
    reg  [3:0] a, b;
    reg  [2:0] op;
    wire [3:0] y;
    wire       carry, zero;
    reg  [3:0] exp_y;
    reg        exp_c;
    integer    ia, ib, iop, errors;

    alu6 dut (.a(a), .b(b), .op(op), .y(y), .carry(carry), .zero(zero));

    initial begin
        errors = 0;
        for (iop = 0; iop < 6; iop = iop + 1)
            for (ia = 0; ia < 16; ia = ia + 1)
                for (ib = 0; ib < 16; ib = ib + 1) begin
                    a = ia; b = ib; op = iop;
                    case (iop)
                        0: begin exp_y = ia + ib;      exp_c = ((ia + ib) > 15); end
                        1: begin exp_y = ia - ib;      exp_c = (ia >= ib);       end
                        2: begin exp_y = ia & ib;      exp_c = 1'b0;             end
                        3: begin exp_y = ia | ib;      exp_c = 1'b0;             end
                        4: begin exp_y = ia ^ ib;      exp_c = 1'b0;             end
                        default: begin exp_y = (ia < ib); exp_c = 1'b0;          end
                    endcase
                    #1;
                    if (y !== exp_y || carry !== exp_c || zero !== (exp_y == 4'd0)) begin
                        errors = errors + 1;
                        $display("FAIL op=%0d a=%0d b=%0d: y=%0d carry=%b", iop, ia, ib, y, carry);
                    end
                end
        if (errors == 0) $display("PASS: %0d cases", 6 * 256);
        else             $display("FAIL: %0d errors", errors);
        $finish;
    end
endmodule

The loops cover \(6 \times 16 \times 16 = 1536\) cases, and a correct design reports PASS: 1536 cases. Values worth checking by hand: \(7 - 9\) gives y = 1110, carry = 0; \(9 - 7\) gives y = 0010, carry = 1; \(5 - 5\) gives y = 0000, zero = 1, carry = 1; \(9 + 9\) gives y = 0010, carry = 1; SLT with \(a = 3\), \(b = 12\) gives y = 0001. A testbench that only drew waveforms would need a person to spot errors, and people miss them among 1 536 cases.

Exercise 5.6. Find the three mistakes in this module, and correct them.

module bad (input wire clk, a, b, c, sel, output reg y, output reg q);
    always @(a or b)
        if (sel) y = a & b & c;
    always @(posedge clk)
        q = y;
endmodule
Answer

First, the sensitivity list (a or b) omits c and sel; write always @(*). Second, y is not assigned when sel = 0, so a latch is inferred; give it a default value or an else. Third, the clocked block uses the blocking assignment =; write q <= y;. Corrected:

module good (input wire clk, a, b, c, sel, output reg y, output reg q);
    always @(*) begin
        y = 1'b0;
        if (sel) y = a & b & c;
    end
    always @(posedge clk)
        q <= y;
endmodule

docs.title: Chapter 3: Verilog: Modules, Signals and Combinational Logic
docs.text: Verilog lets you describe a digital circuit as text. It looks like a programming language, but it is not one, and getting that straight first saves weeks of confusion. This chapter explains what kind of language Verilog is, introduces the module and its ports, the two kinds of signal and the four values a bit can carry, then shows the three styles in which the same circuit can be written and the construct, always @(*), that you will use for most combinational logic. The chapter ends with the first of the two assignment operators, whose proper use is the subject of the next chapter.

docs.title: 3.1 A language for describing hardware
docs.text:
A hardware description language lets you write down a circuit as text. Verilog, standardised as IEEE 1364 and later folded into SystemVerilog, is one; VHDL, the subject of Chapters 6 and 7, is the other. In both, you describe what the circuit is: its registers, its logic and how they connect. Every line ends up as wires and flip-flops, not as instructions to a processor, and so all of it is active at the same time, as all the components on a circuit board are.

Compare a C program with a Verilog description:

x = a + b;   /* first this  */
y = x * 2;   /* then this   */
z = y - 1;   /* then this   */

assign z = y - 1;   // all three exist together,
assign x = a + b;   // in any order
assign y = x * 2;

The C program is run by one processor, line after line, and the order of the lines is the order of events. The three Verilog lines are three pieces of circuitry, all present at once; shuffle them and you describe exactly the same hardware. A program is a recipe, with one cook doing one step at a time. A Verilog description is an orchestra in which every player plays all the time, and what you write is the score that says how they connect.

A Verilog description has two uses.

  • Simulation. A program pretends to be the circuit and runs it over simulated time, so that you can test the design before it exists. Icarus Verilog, Verilator and ModelSim are simulators.
  • Synthesis. A tool turns your description into a netlist of real gates and flip-flops. Yosys, Vivado and Quartus are synthesis tools.

Everything can be simulated, but only a subset can be synthesised

A line such as #10 ("wait 10 time units") is fine in a simulation and meaningless in silicon, since a chip cannot wait a chosen number of nanoseconds on command. Constructs used to build test environments (delays, printing, file input) are not synthesizable. This book marks them when they appear.

docs.title: 3.2 Modules and ports
docs.text:
The building block of Verilog is the module. It has a name, a list of ports (its pins, the connections to the outside world) and a body that says how its outputs depend on its inputs.

// A module: name, ports, body. Comments use // or /* ... */
module and_gate (
    input  wire a,      // input port
    input  wire b,
    output wire y       // output port
);
    assign y = a & b;   // continuous assignment: y is always a AND b
endmodule

From outside, a module is a black box with pins. Larger designs place modules inside modules, like chips on a board, to form a hierarchy. Everything in a module's body happens concurrently, unless it sits inside a procedural block (Section 3.5).

Every port has a direction, written before its name.

Direction Meaning Typical use input driven from outside, read inside clocks, data in, control output driven inside, read outside results, status flags inout both ways; a tri-state line shared buses, chip pins

docs.title: 3.3 Signals and the values they carry
wire and reg
docs.text:
Verilog has two kinds of signal, and the difference between them is the most common beginner confusion.

wire (a net) reg (a variable) Gets its value from an assign, or a module output an assignment inside always or initial Holds a value? no: it always shows whatever drives it yes: it keeps the last value given to it Becomes a flip-flop? never only if it is assigned on a clock edge

A reg is not necessarily a register

The keyword reg does not mean "register". It means "assigned inside a procedural block". A reg written in a combinational block becomes plain gates. SystemVerilog renamed it logic to end the confusion, and a good habit is to read reg as "variable".

docs.title: Four values
docs.text:
A Verilog bit has four values, not two, which models real hardware more faithfully.

Value Meaning 0 logic low; false; ground 1 logic high; true x unknown: never set, or two drivers disagree z high impedance: not driven at all (tri-state, disconnected)

An x in simulation is the simulator telling you that it does not know a value, usually a register that was never reset or two outputs fighting. Real hardware would quietly pick a 0 or a 1 and fail some days but not others. Hunt down every x: x & 1 is x because the bit might be 0 or 1.

docs.title: Number literals
docs.text:
A sized literal is written width ' base digits: the number of bits, then the base (b binary, o octal, d decimal, h hexadecimal), then the digits. Underscores are ignored and help reading.

4'b1010                    // 4-bit binary  = decimal 10
8'hFF                      // 8-bit hex     = 255 (all ones)
6'o17                      // 6-bit octal   = 15
12'd2048                   // 12-bit decimal
16'b1010_1100_0011_0001    // underscores for readability
8'bxxxx_zzzz               // partly unknown, partly high-impedance

Example 3.1: widths in literals

What does 4'd17 hold, and what is 8'hA5 in binary?

  1. The number 17 needs five bits (10001), but the literal is only four bits wide, so the top bit is dropped and 4'd17 holds 0001, which is 1. This is a classic silent bug.
  2. Each hexadecimal digit is exactly four bits: A is 1010 and 5 is 0101, so 8'hA5 = 1010_0101.

docs.title: 3.4 Three ways to write the same circuit
docs.text:
Verilog offers three styles for describing a circuit, at different levels of abstraction. To compare them we describe the same 2-to-1 multiplexer in each. Its output \(y\) copies \(a\) when \(sel = 0\) and \(b\) when \(sel = 1\):

\[y = \overline{sel}\cdot a + sel \cdot b\]

docs.title: Dataflow: assign
docs.text:
The circuit is described as Boolean equations on wires. A continuous assignment, assign, says "this wire is always equal to this expression": whenever an input changes, y follows. Here ~ is NOT, & is AND, | is OR and ^ is XOR.

module mux2_dataflow (
    input  wire a,
    input  wire b,
    input  wire sel,
    output wire y
);
    assign y = (~sel & a) | (sel & b);
    // or simply:  assign y = sel ? b : a;
endmodule

docs.title: Structural: instantiate gates
docs.text:
The circuit is described as a netlist of named gates, wired together, which is as close to a schematic (Figure 3.1) as text can be. Verilog has built-in primitives and, or, not, nand, nor, xor, xnor and buf. Each line creates an instance, one copy of a building block with its own name, and for built-in gates the output comes first.

module mux2_structural (
    input  wire a, b, sel,
    output wire y
);
    wire nsel, a_sel, b_sel;     // internal wires
    not  g1 (nsel,  sel);        // nsel  = ~sel
    and  g2 (a_sel, a, nsel);    // a_sel = a & ~sel
    and  g3 (b_sel, b, sel);     // b_sel = b & sel
    or   g4 (y, a_sel, b_sel);   // y     = a_sel | b_sel
endmodule
Figure 3.1. The 2-to-1 multiplexer as a netlist of four gates. The structural Verilog description is this diagram written as text.

For your own modules, connect ports by name, which is independent of the order of the ports and documents itself: mux2 u1 (.a(x), .b(y), .sel(s), .y(out));.

docs.title: Behavioural: always blocks
docs.text:
The circuit is described by what it does, and synthesis works out the gates. An always block holds statements that run whenever something they watch changes. Here @(*) means "any input".

module mux2_behavioural (
    input  wire a, b, sel,
    output reg  y            // assigned inside always, so it is a reg
);
    always @(*) begin
        if (sel) y = b;
        else     y = a;
    end
endmodule

docs.title: Which to use?
docs.text:
Style Describes Best for For a 32-bit mux Dataflow equations small combinational logic change one width Structural gates and their wiring joining big blocks together dozens of hand-wired gates Behavioural what it does nearly everything else change one width

All three synthesise to the same circuit. Real designs mix them: behaviour inside each block, structure to connect the blocks.

docs.title: 3.5 Combinational logic with always @(*)
docs.text:
Combinational logic has outputs that depend only on the inputs right now, with no memory. For anything more complicated than an equation, write it as always @(*). What follows the @ is the sensitivity list, the signals whose change makes the block run again; @(*) builds the list automatically from every signal the block reads. Inside, use the plain assignment =. And give every output a value on every path through the block (Section 5.5 explains why).

// a 4-to-1 multiplexer with case
module mux4 (
    input  wire [1:0] sel,
    input  wire       a, b, c, d,
    output reg        y
);
    always @(*) begin
        case (sel)
            2'b00:   y = a;
            2'b01:   y = b;
            2'b10:   y = c;
            2'b11:   y = d;
            default: y = 1'bx;     // good hygiene, even if unreachable
        endcase
    end
endmodule

A chain of if ... else if gives priority: the first test that is true wins. A case treats its choices as equals. A 2-to-4 decoder with an enable shows the priority of an if chain:

module decoder2to4 (
    input  wire       en,
    input  wire [1:0] in,
    output reg  [3:0] out
);
    always @(*) begin
        if (!en)              out = 4'b0000;
        else if (in == 2'b00) out = 4'b0001;
        else if (in == 2'b01) out = 4'b0010;
        else if (in == 2'b10) out = 4'b0100;
        else                  out = 4'b1000;
    end
endmodule

Its behaviour is the truth table

en in out 0 xx 0000 1 00 0001 1 01 0010 1 10 0100 1 11 1000

and the first row shows the priority at work: en = 0 overrides everything below it.

docs.title: 3.6 Two kinds of assignment
docs.text:
Inside procedural blocks Verilog has two assignment operators, and choosing the wrong one is the commonest cause of designs that simulate correctly and fail in hardware.

Blocking = Non-blocking <= When it happens immediately, line by line, like software all right-hand sides are read first; all left-hand sides update together Models combinational logic clocked logic (registers) Use it in always @(*) always @(posedge clk)

The second column is the RTL rule of Chapter 1: in one clock pulse, read everything, then write everything. The operator <= is the RTL arrow. The rule that prevents most bugs is:

The rule

Use blocking = in combinational always @(*) blocks. Use non-blocking <= in sequential always @(posedge clk) blocks. Never mix the two in one block.

The difference is visible in the swap of two registers on a clock edge:

always @(posedge clk) begin      // non-blocking: a true swap
    a <= b;
    b <= a;                      // both right-hand sides read the OLD values
end

always @(posedge clk) begin      // blocking: NOT a swap
    a = b;
    b = a;                       // a was already overwritten: both become old b
end

The next chapter applies the rule to flip-flops, counters and state machines.

docs.title: 3.7 Summary
docs.text:
• Verilog describes hardware: modules exist and work all at once; they are not run line by line. A description is used for simulation and, in a synthesizable subset, for synthesis.
  • A module has ports (input, output, inout) and a body. Larger designs instantiate modules inside modules, connecting ports by name.
  • A wire is driven continuously; a reg is assigned in a block and is not automatically a flip-flop. Bits are 0, 1, x (unknown) or z (high impedance).
  • Literals are written width, base, digits; a literal that is too narrow loses its top bits silently.
  • The three styles, dataflow (assign), structural (instances) and behavioural (always), describe the same hardware. Real designs mix them.
  • Combinational logic: always @(*) with blocking =, and every output assigned on every path.
  • Sequential logic: always @(posedge clk) with non-blocking <=.

docs.title: 3.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 3.1. Give the value of each literal as a decimal number, or the binary pattern where that is clearer: 8'hA5, 4'd17, 6'o17, 5'b1_0110.

Answer

8'hA5 is 1010_0101, which is 165 in decimal. 4'd17 needs five bits and the literal has four, so it holds 0001, which is 1. 6'o17 is octal 17, which is \(1 \times 8 + 7 = 15\), written 001111 in six bits. 5'b1_0110 is 10110, which is 22 (the underscore is ignored).

Exercise 3.2. Given wire [7:0] data = 8'b1001_0110; and wire [3:0] nibble = 4'b1011;, give the value of: (a) {data[6:0], data[7]}; (b) {4'b0000, nibble}; (c) {{4{nibble[3]}}, nibble}; (d) data[3:0].

Answer

(a) A rotate left by one: the seven low bits 001_0110 followed by the old top bit 1 give 0010_1101. (b) Zero-extension: 0000_1011. (c) Sign extension: the sign bit nibble[3] is 1, so four copies of it are placed in front: 1111_1011, which is \(-5\) again in 8 bits. (d) The part-select of the low four bits is 0110.

Exercise 3.3. Write a 3-input majority function (output 1 when at least two inputs are 1) in dataflow style, and give its truth table.

Answer 
module majority3 (input wire a, b, c, output wire y);
    assign y = (a & b) | (a & c) | (b & c);
endmodule
a b c y 000 0 001 0 010 0 011 1 100 0 101 1 110 1 111 1

This is the same expression that gives the carry-out of a full adder (Chapter 5).

Exercise 3.4. The following block is meant to be combinational. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

always @(*) begin
    if (sel) y = a;
end
Answer

When sel = 0 nothing assigns y, so y must remember its old value. Memory in a combinational block means that synthesis builds a latch, which is almost never wanted and a source of timing trouble. Two fixes: give y a default value first (y = 1'b0; if (sel) y = a;), or provide a complete else (else y = 1'b0;). Either way, every path now gives y a value, and the block is pure combinational logic.

Exercise 3.5. Write a priority encoder: a 4-bit input req and a 2-bit output idx giving the position of the highest bit that is set, plus a one-bit valid that is 0 when no bit is set.

Answer 
module prio4 (
    input  wire [3:0] req,
    output reg  [1:0] idx,
    output reg        valid
);
    always @(*) begin
        valid = 1'b1;
        if      (req[3]) idx = 2'd3;
        else if (req[2]) idx = 2'd2;
        else if (req[1]) idx = 2'd1;
        else if (req[0]) idx = 2'd0;
        else begin
            idx   = 2'd0;
            valid = 1'b0;
        end
    end
endmodule

The if chain supplies the priority (bit 3 beats bit 2, and so on), and both outputs are assigned on every path, so no latch is inferred. For req = 4'b0110 the output is idx = 2, valid = 1.

Exercise 3.6. Why is y = (~sel & a) | (sel & b) easy to widen to a 32-bit multiplexer when written as assign y = sel ? b : a; with 32-bit vectors, while the structural version is not?

Answer

The conditional operator works on whole vectors, so widening the multiplexer means changing the declarations of a, b and y to 32 bits; the single line stays the same. The structural version names every gate, so a 32-bit multiplexer needs 32 copies of the four-gate group, 128 hand-wired gates, each with its own wires. Structure is for joining big blocks, not for describing logic that an equation or a behaviour describes in one line.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Verilog: Sequential Logic and State Machines
docs.text: Combinational logic has no memory; sequential logic does. This chapter shows how flip-flops, registers, shift registers and counters are written in Verilog, how reset works, and how to build a finite state machine with a three-block template that keeps the design readable and synthesizable. The running example is a detector for the bit pattern 1-0-1, built twice, first as a Moore machine and then as a Mealy machine, so that the difference between them can be seen in a waveform.

docs.title: 4.1 The flip-flop: one bit of memory
docs.text:
Sequential logic has memory: its outputs depend on what happened at earlier clock edges. The template for it is an always block triggered by a clock edge, with non-blocking assignments (Section 3.6).

module dff (
    input  wire clk, d,
    output reg  q
);
    always @(posedge clk)
        q <= d;          // on each rising edge, q captures d
endmodule

The output q takes the value that d had at each rising edge and holds it until the next one. A short pulse on d that comes and goes between two edges is never seen by q. The physical remembering happens in the flip-flop that synthesis builds for q; any logic between flip-flops is purely combinational.

docs.title: 4.2 Registers with load and reset
docs.text:
A register that keeps its value unless told to load a new one is the most common sequential building block. Real designs also need a way of putting every register into a known state, a reset.

module reg8 (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       rst_n,    // active-low asynchronous reset
    input  wire       load,     // synchronous load enable
    input  wire [7:0] d,
    output reg  [7:0] q
);
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)      q <= 8'h00;   // async: acts the instant rst_n drops
        else if (load)   q <= d;       // sync: only on a clock edge
        // else: q holds its value (implied)
    end
endmodule

Several points are packed into these few lines.

  • The name rst_n uses the convention _n for "active when 0".
  • An asynchronous reset appears in the sensitivity list (or negedge rst_n), so it acts the instant it arrives, without waiting for the clock. A synchronous reset is tested inside the clocked block only and takes effect at the next edge. Choose one convention per design and keep to it.
  • With no else, q simply holds. In a clocked block, that is exactly what a register with an enable does, and it does not create a latch.

Figure 4.1 shows reg8 at work. The register loads 3C and then A5 on ordinary edges. Between the second and third edges rst_n drops, and q becomes 00 at that very moment, because the reset is asynchronous. At the third edge, rst_n is back to 1 and load is 1, so q loads A5 again. At the last edge load = 0, so q keeps A5 although d has changed to 77.

Figure 4.1. A register with asynchronous reset and synchronous load. The reset clears q between clock edges; with load low, q holds.

docs.title: 4.3 Shift registers and counters
docs.text:
A shift register moves every bit one place along on each edge. This 4-bit serial-in, parallel-out register turns a stream of bits that arrive one at a time into a 4-bit word, which is how serial links receive data.

module shift_reg4 (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       rst_n,
    input  wire       sin,       // serial input bit
    output reg  [3:0] q
);
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n) q <= 4'b0000;
        else        q <= {q[2:0], sin};   // shift left; sin enters at bit 0
    end
endmodule

The braces { , } join bits, with the first item on the left; no logic is built, only wiring (Section 5.1).

Example 4.1: filling the shift register

Start with q = 0000 and feed sin = 1, 0, 1, 1 on four successive edges. At each edge the old q[2:0] moves up one place and the new bit enters at the bottom.

Edge sin q before {q[2:0], sin} q after 1 1 0000 000 followed by 1 0001 2 0 0001 001 followed by 0 0010 3 1 0010 010 followed by 1 0101 4 1 0101 101 followed by 1 1011

After four edges q = 1011: the first bit that arrived is now in the top position, so the stream has been assembled into a word with the earliest bit most significant.

Shift registers are the heart of serial links. A UART (the asynchronous serial port found on almost every microcontroller) sends a byte as a frame: the line rests at 1, a start bit 0 announces the frame, the eight data bits follow with the least significant first, and a stop bit 1 ends it (Figure 4.2). A transmitter is a shift register loaded with the whole frame and emptied one bit per bit-time; Exercise 4.6 asks you to build one.

Figure 4.2. A UART frame carrying 0x41: idle high, a start bit, eight data bits with the least significant first, and a stop bit.

The counter of Chapter 1 is now complete, with reset and wrap-around:

module counter8 (
    input  wire       clk,
    input  wire       rst_n,
    input  wire       en,
    output reg  [7:0] count
);
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n)   count <= 8'h00;
        else if (en)  count <= count + 1'b1;   // wraps 255 -> 0 by itself
    end
endmodule

The eight flip-flops hold count; the adder is plain combinational logic between their outputs and their inputs. It is the clock edge that turns count + 1 into a counter rather than an endless loop.

docs.title: 4.4 Finite state machines
docs.text:
A finite state machine is the heart of almost every controller. We design the "101" detector, which receives one bit per clock on din and raises found for one cycle whenever the last three bits were 1, 0, 1. Overlaps count: the final 1 of one pattern may start the next, so the stream 1-0-1-0-1 contains two detections.

Clock edge 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 din 1 0 1 0 1 1 0 found (ideal) 0 0 1 0 1 0 0

The machine must remember enough of the past to see this. Each state records how much of the pattern has been seen so far: nothing useful (S_IDLE), a 1 (S_1), a 1 followed by a 0 (S_10), or the whole pattern (S_101). Draw the states first (Figure 4.3), then write the code.

Figure 4.3. State diagram of the Moore 101 detector. found is 1 only in S_101. The arrow from S_101 on din = 1 goes back to S_1, because that 1 may start the next pattern.

The clean, synthesis-friendly template has three blocks: a clocked block for the state register, a combinational block for the next-state logic, and combinational logic for the outputs.

module seq_detect_101 (
    input  wire clk,
    input  wire rst_n,
    input  wire din,          // serial data in, one bit per clock
    output reg  found         // pulses high when 101 is detected
);
    // state encoding: parameters make it readable
    localparam [1:0] S_IDLE = 2'b00,   // seen nothing useful
                     S_1    = 2'b01,   // seen "1"
                     S_10   = 2'b10,   // seen "10"
                     S_101  = 2'b11;   // seen "101": detected

    reg [1:0] state, next;

    // 1) state register (sequential)
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n) state <= S_IDLE;
        else        state <= next;
    end

    // 2) next-state logic (combinational)
    always @(*) begin
        next = state;                       // default: stay
        case (state)
            S_IDLE: next = din ? S_1   : S_IDLE;
            S_1:    next = din ? S_1   : S_10;
            S_10:   next = din ? S_101 : S_IDLE;
            S_101:  next = din ? S_1   : S_10;   // overlap: this 1 starts anew
            default: next = S_IDLE;
        endcase
    end

    // 3) output logic (combinational; Moore: depends on the state only)
    always @(*) begin
        found = (state == S_101);
    end
endmodule

The state register is the only clocked block and holds where we are. The next-state logic reads the arrows of the diagram. The output logic is combinational: here found is 1 only in S_101. Naming the state codes with localparam makes the code read like the diagram.

Example 4.2: running the detector

Feed the stream 1 0 1 0 1 1 0 1, one bit per edge, starting from S_IDLE.

Edge din State before State after found while in the new state 1 1 S_IDLE S_1 0 2 0 S_1 S_10 0 3 1 S_10 S_101 1 4 0 S_101 S_10 0 5 1 S_10 S_101 1 6 1 S_101 S_1 0 7 0 S_1 S_10 0 8 1 S_10 S_101 1

Three detections, completed by the bits at edges 3, 5 and 8. The detection at edge 5 uses the 1 at edge 3 as its first bit: this is the overlap that the arrow from S_101 to S_1 (or, after a 0, to S_10) provides.

docs.title: Moore and Mealy machines
docs.text:
In a Moore machine the outputs depend only on the state. The detector above is one, and its output is glitch-free and changes only at clock edges. In a Mealy machine the outputs depend on the state and the inputs, so the machine can react one cycle sooner and often needs fewer states, but a glitch on an input can reach the output. The three-block template supports both: only the output block changes.

The Mealy detector needs only three states, since it can raise found in the cycle in which the final 1 is present on din, without waiting for a fourth state:

module seq_detect_101_mealy (
    input  wire clk, rst_n, din,
    output reg  found
);
    localparam [1:0] S_IDLE = 2'd0, S_1 = 2'd1, S_10 = 2'd2;
    reg [1:0] state, next;

    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
        if (!rst_n) state <= S_IDLE;
        else        state <= next;

    always @(*) begin
        next  = state;          // defaults: stay, no detection
        found = 1'b0;
        case (state)
            S_IDLE: if (din) next = S_1;
            S_1:    if (!din) next = S_10;      // din = 1: stay in S_1
            S_10:   if (din) begin
                        found = 1'b1;           // 101 completes right now
                        next  = S_1;            // this 1 may start another
                    end else next = S_IDLE;
            default: next = S_IDLE;
        endcase
    end
endmodule

Figure 4.4 compares the two on the same input. The Mealy found rises while the last 1 is still on din; the Moore found follows one clock later, once the machine has moved into S_101.

Figure 4.4. The Moore and Mealy detectors on the same input stream. Mealy found goes high one clock earlier than Moore found; Moore needs four states, Mealy three.

docs.title: 4.5 Summary
docs.text:
• A flip-flop is written always @(posedge clk) q <= d;. Everything assigned on a clock edge becomes a flip-flop; the logic between flip-flops is combinational.
  • A register with no assignment on some path simply holds; in a clocked block this is a register with enable, not a latch.
  • An asynchronous reset is in the sensitivity list (or negedge rst_n) and acts at once; a synchronous reset is tested inside the clocked block and acts at the next edge.
  • Shift registers use concatenation; counters wrap by themselves when they run out of bits.
  • Build state machines with the three-block template: state register, next-state logic with a default, output logic. Name the states with localparam.
  • A Moore machine's outputs follow the state; a Mealy machine's outputs also follow the inputs, so they appear one clock earlier and the machine can be smaller.

docs.title: 4.6 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 4.1 (a counter with load and enable). Write a counter with inputs clk, an asynchronous active-low rst_n, load, en and d[7:0], and output q[7:0]. The priority is reset, then load, then count. Make the width a parameter. Check by hand: after reset, enable for 10 clocks; then load 250; then enable for 10 more clocks; then hold en = 0 for three clocks. What is q after each step, and what happens at 4 bits?

Answer 
module counter_ld #(parameter W = 8) (
    input  wire         clk, rst_n, load, en,
    input  wire [W-1:0] d,
    output reg  [W-1:0] q
);
    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
        if (!rst_n)      q <= {W{1'b0}};
        else if (load)   q <= d;
        else if (en)     q <= q + 1'b1;
endmodule

The order of the if tests gives the priority. Hand check: after 10 counts, \(q = 10\). After the load, \(q = 250\). After 10 more counts, \(250 + 10 = 260\), and \(260 \bmod 256 = 4\), since the register wraps after 255. With en = 0 for three clocks it stays at 4. At 4 bits (W = 4), ten counts from 0 give 10, and six more give \(16 \bmod 16 = 0\).

Exercise 4.2. A 4-bit shift register shift_reg4 starts at 0000. The serial input over six edges is 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0. Give q after each edge.

Answer

Each edge computes {q[2:0], sin}: 0001, then 0011, then 0110, then 1100, then 1001 (the old 100 followed by 1), then 0010 (the old 001 followed by 0).

Exercise 4.3. In the register of Figure 4.1, why is rst_n in the sensitivity list while load is not? What would change if the reset were synchronous?

Answer

The reset is asynchronous, so the block must wake up the moment rst_n changes, independently of the clock. load is only sampled on the clock edge, inside the clocked branch, so it needs no place in the sensitivity list. A synchronous reset would be removed from the list (always @(posedge clk)); the clear would then happen only at the next rising edge, and a reset pulse shorter than a clock period could be missed.

Exercise 4.4 (the 101 detector). (a) Run the Moore detector on the stream 1 1 0 1 0 1 1 0 1 and count the detections. (b) State when the Mealy version's output rises compared with the Moore version's, and how many states each needs.

Answer

(a) Number the bits 1 to 9: 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1. The pattern 1-0-1 is completed by bits 2-3-4, by bits 4-5-6 and by bits 7-8-9, so the detections end at bits 4, 6 and 9: three in all. (b) The Moore output goes high in the cycle after the last 1 arrives. The Mealy output goes high in the same cycle as the last 1, one clock earlier. The Moore machine needs four states; the Mealy machine needs three.

Exercise 4.5. The Moore detector's S_101 state goes to S_1 on din = 1 and to S_10 on din = 0. Why not to S_IDLE in both cases? Which stream would fail?

Answer

The final 1 of a detected 101 can be the first 1 of the next pattern, and the 0 after it can continue "1-0". Sending S_101 to S_IDLE would forget that bit and miss overlapping patterns. The stream 1 0 1 0 1 would give one detection instead of two.

Exercise 4.6 (a UART transmitter). Design a block with inputs clk, rst_n, start, data[7:0] and tick (one pulse per bit time) and outputs tx and busy. On start it sends a start bit 0, the eight data bits lowest first, and a stop bit 1; the line rests at 1. Give the sequence on tx for data = 8'h41.

Answer

\(\text{0x41} = 0100\,0001\). Sent lowest bit first, the line carries, tick by tick: start 0, then bits 0 to 7 which are 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, then stop 1. That is 0 | 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 | 1, ten bit times in all.

One design keeps the whole frame in a 10-bit shift register and a counter of the bits that remain:

module uart_tx (
    input  wire       clk, rst_n,
    input  wire       start,
    input  wire [7:0] data,
    input  wire       tick,          // one pulse per bit time
    output reg        tx,
    output wire       busy
);
    reg [3:0] cnt;                   // 0 = idle, 1..10 = bits still to send
    reg [9:0] frame;                 // {stop, data[7:0], start}, sent LSB first
    assign busy = (cnt != 4'd0);

    always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
        if (!rst_n) begin
            tx <= 1'b1; cnt <= 4'd0; frame <= 10'h3FF;
        end else if (cnt == 4'd0) begin
            if (start) begin
                frame <= {1'b1, data, 1'b0};
                cnt   <= 4'd10;
            end
        end else if (tick) begin
            tx    <= frame[0];                  // next bit onto the line
            frame <= {1'b1, frame[9:1]};        // shift, filling with 1
            cnt   <= cnt - 4'd1;
        end
    end
endmodule

The line stays at 1 until the first tick, when the start bit 0 is placed on it; each later tick places the next bit, the tenth being the stop bit. busy is high from the accepted start until the tenth tick. To test it, make tick a pulse every four clocks, send 8'h41, and sample tx at each tick: the sequence above must appear.

docs.title: Chapter 6: VHDL: Entities, Architectures and Processes
docs.text: VHDL, the VHSIC Hardware Description Language, describes the same hardware as Verilog, but in a different spirit. It is strongly typed, deliberately verbose and reads like a contract: you say exactly what each signal is, and the compiler refuses to guess. This chapter introduces the two halves of every design (entity and architecture), the libraries and types that nearly every design uses, the concurrent statements that describe wires, and the process, the construct that holds sequential statements. It ends with the one idea that newcomers find hardest, the difference between a signal and a variable. The next chapter builds registers, state machines, arithmetic and testbenches.

docs.title: 6.1 Entity and architecture
docs.text:
VHDL was created in the 1980s for the United States VHSIC programme and standardised as IEEE 1076. As with Verilog, it has two uses: synthesis, for a subset that maps to real gates and flip-flops, and simulation, for the full language, including testbenches that cannot be built in silicon.

Every VHDL design has two halves (Figure 6.1).

  • The entity is the black box: its name and its ports (the pins), each with a name, a direction and a type.
  • The architecture is the inside: the logic that drives the outputs. One entity can have several architectures (behavioural, structural, RTL), and you choose one when you instantiate the entity.
Figure 6.1. An entity declares the ports; an architecture holds the concurrent statements and processes that implement them. 
-- The interface: a 2-input AND gate
entity and2 is
    port (
        a : in  std_logic;     -- input port
        b : in  std_logic;     -- input port
        y : out std_logic      -- output port (no ';' after the last port)
    );
end entity and2;

-- One implementation of that interface
architecture rtl of and2 is
begin
    y <= a and b;              -- a concurrent signal assignment
end architecture rtl;

Port directions, called modes, are in, out, inout and buffer.

docs.title: 6.2 Libraries and types
docs.text:
Almost every real design opens with the IEEE library and two packages:

library ieee;
use ieee.std_logic_1164.all;    -- std_logic, std_logic_vector, rising_edge
use ieee.numeric_std.all;       -- unsigned, signed, to_integer, to_unsigned

The package std_logic_1164 provides the nine-valued logic type; numeric_std provides typed arithmetic on vectors. Do not use the old vendor packages std_logic_arith, std_logic_unsigned or std_logic_signed: they are not standard and clash with numeric_std.

docs.title: std_logic and strong typing
docs.text:
The type std_logic is not just 0 and 1. It resolves several drivers on one wire and models real electrical states.

Value Meaning Value Meaning '0' strong drive low 'Z' high impedance (tri-state) '1' strong drive high 'W' weak unknown 'U' uninitialised 'L' weak 0 (pull-down) 'X' strong unknown, or a conflict 'H' weak 1 (pull-up) '-' don't care

A std_logic_vector is a bundle of these bits, for example std_logic_vector(7 downto 0) for a byte.
